Why The Rings of Power Will Never Be the Same After the Season 3 Finale

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1646 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Esquire

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that when the creators and showrunners of The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power embarked on season 3, they knew the endgame from the start: The forging of the One Ring.
  • “We wanted a tighter, tauter, more profound season,” indicates co-showrunner Patrick McKay, in an interview with Esquire.
  • It has been revealed that “We had to have Sauron forge the One Ring,” adds J.D.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that when the creators and showrunners of The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power embarked on season 3, they knew the endgame from the start: The forging of the One Ring. After two seasons in the Second Age of Middle-earth, which saw almost all the other Rings of Power forged—three for Elves, seven for Dwarves, and nine for Men—it was time for Sauron to forge the one to rule them all.

“We wanted a tighter, tauter, more profound season,” indicates co-showrunner Patrick McKay, in an interview with Esquire. “We wanted to start with a bang and never let up. We wanted to deepen our characters psychologically, and challenge them in new ways. You’re seeing the end of one part of the story, and the beginning of another.”.

It has been revealed that “We had to have Sauron forge the One Ring,” adds J.D. Payne, who also created and serves as co-showrunner with McKay. “To do that, all the storylines in some way are connected to Sauron’s attempts at world domination. That was the one that so much of our attention and focus went into getting right, and it took all of our departments working together at the top of their games to create.”.

On Wednesday, just in time for Thanksgiving, Prime Video gave Tolkien fans a feast with the final two episodes of The Rings of Power season 3: episode 7, “Orodruin,” and episode 8, “The Doom of Men.”.

In a recent development, in the penultimate episode, Sauron (Charlie Vickers) learns from the Balrog—who talks, apparently!—how to use the fires of Mount Doom to forge the One Ring. Then, with the power of the One Ring literally in his hands, Sauron mobilizes his army for battle against Pharazôn (Trystan Gravelle), the king of Númenor. But instead of a big, violent bloodbath in the spirit of, say, Game of Thrones, Sauron simply... surrenders. Or does he? We’re talking about a master deceiver, after all.

In a spoiler-filled interview with Esquire, McKay and Payne unpack a few of our biggest questions about season 3, including how and why the Balrog speaks (with actor Simon Pegg lending his voice) to why Pharazôn is actually one of the most consequential figures in the series.

This interview has been edited for clarity.

ESQUIRE: So, wait, the Balrog can talk?

In a recent development, PATRICK MCKAY: One of the things we're constantly trying to do is go deeper into Tolkien’s life's work. He did not just create The Lord of the Rings, he wrote all this other stuff. He envisioned an entire world. It's his legendarium. When you do the deep dive, you find there are surprising things if you only know the book and film trilogy. The Balrog Gandalf faces down in Moria is part of this level of “super being” that is equal to Gandalf and Sauron. They’re Maiar. In prior ages, Balrogs could cast spells and command troops. They’re intelligent. They can talk, you just don’t see that one talk in that circumstance.

The idea of walking out onto a diving board and doing something risky, to show a different side of that being, was something that we felt compelled to do this season. It’s certainly unexpected. We’re always looking to do that. We don’t want to be familiar. We want to show you things in this world that you haven’t seen before.

Talk to me about designing a upcoming One Ring. Granted, it’s a gold ring; there’s not much you can really deviate. But in what ways did you want to create a One Ring that belongs to The Rings of Power?

In a recent development, MCKAY: The books are pretty specific about the way it looks. It’s a plain gold band. If you’re gonna do that, it’s going to look like the One Ring you’ve seen in other adaptations. We did make a few modifications, just for camera. We broadened it to give it more chunkiness. But it is what it notes on the tin.

How is season 3 a culmination of everything that’s happened before, and how is it setting up the rest of the show?

Sources indicate that J.D. PAYNE: It pulls together everything we’ve been doing with Sauron and Galadriel from the first two seasons. In season 1, he befriended her and deceived her in the guise of Halbrand. In season 3, you see Celebrimbor tormenting him: “You’re never gonna be able to make a ring capable of dominating all the other rings—or dominating her.” Part of Sauron’s ambition to forge the One Ring, as a character motivation, is being able to dominate the person who stated “no” to him over the last few seasons. You understand how crazy that must have driven him.

According to recent reports, MCKAY: The show’s called Rings of Power, because the creation is the throughline of this entire era of Tolkien’s mythology. At the end of season 3, you’ve now seen the creation of all of them. That’s now the world we live in. Everyone in Middle-earth is a nuclear power, so to speak. Now we’re setting up for the next part of the story, which is, “What are the consequences going to be?” One thing in season 3 we really invested in was Númenor to set Sauron up as the bowling ball crashing into those pins. That’s sort of the beginning of the end of the Second Age. It’s a tragic story. The Rings have an impact on Middle-earth that is felt for thousands of years. Now they are in this world.

In a recent development, the finale is literally titled “The Doom of Men,” and it ends with Sauron “surrendering” to Pharazôn. Or so that’s what he wants them to think. Can you break down this moment? How is this Sauron’s big chess move?

It has been revealed that PAYNE: Everything builds up to that. You’ve seen Gandalf getting through to the Dark Wizard and take out a massive portion of Sauron’s army at the last moment. So the game changes right from underneath him, and he has to make a calculation. Is he going to put all his chips on the table and lose his army in a stalemate? Or is there another way? The great thing about Sauron is that he’s amazing at constructing scenarios that are lose-lose. If he can’t beat Pharazôn on the field of battle, he reasons maybe there’s another way. That’s why the final moment is filled with tension. It’s not simply a surrender. Our Elves, particularly Galadriel, know Sauron so well. She knows this is not a defeat for Sauron, and he’s going to find a way to make this into a play for exactly what he wants. Those who know the lore know what happens when Sauron is taken prisoner to Númenor. We wanted that feeling of dread, watching Charlie Vickers have a hint of a smile.

Industry observers note that one of the most consequential characters this season has been Pharazôn. In what ways does Pharazôn represent the downfall of man?

MCKAY: This is a major character in the mythology. We introduced him in season 1, he’s been sort of a politician gathering power. In season 3, he’s been king for five days, and he’s in his heyday. He’s in his golden era. But he’s driven by insecurity. There was this blacksmith we empowered, who got away, who’s now marching around saying he’s “Lord.” No, I’m the guy! There’s professional jealousy there.

Industry observers note that we talk sometimes about how he’s Stalin to Sauron’s Hitler. You’ve got two characters who are quite full of themselves, and have a high opinion of themselves, which puts them on a trajectory. Pharazôn’s goal is, “I want to take on Sauron.” That makes him a compelling character because you watch the way he greases the wheels and maneuvers to bring about that end. We give a lot of credit to our actor, Trystan Gravelle. He leaps off the screen in season 3.

Speaking of showdowns, one of the biggest confrontations you stage in season 3 is between Sauron and Gandalf, which Tolkien never wrote in the books. What did you hope to discover by pitting these characters together?

MCKAY: The journey of Gandalf and his involvement with Ciaran Hinds’ character, Pollando, has real deep roots in some Tolkien deep cuts where he talked about wizards who went east and that their activities probably prevented the east from joining Sauron. The story comes from that. We wanted to dramatize that through some of the most iconic characters in the legendarium coming face to face.

Sources indicate that PAYNE: Seeing the contrast between them felt like too delicious an opportunity to pass up. Sauron is seeking power at all costs, and Gandalf has been told by the Secret Fire, “To access the greatest power in the universe, you have to give up all other power.” So when Gandalf is offered the world by Sauron, he turns it down. If you demand power, it’s going to destroy you. Ultimately, having the One Ring, and forging it and trying to keep power, sets up the weaknesses of the Third Age that the heroes exploit to finally destroy Sauron.

In a recent development, one of my favorite hobbies is Magic: The Gathering, which has had both Lord of the Rings and The Hobbit as crossover sets. Are there any possibilities for a Rings of Power collaboration?

It has been revealed that MCKAY: [Laughs.] No. This is the first we’ve heard about it.

In a recent development, PAYNE: We actually wrote a draft of a Magic: The Gathering script in the before times. It was one of the last scripts we worked on before turning to Rings of Power. But it was right before the Disney-Fox merger, and it kinda got lost there. But we love that universe.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A swipe of lipstick is one of the easiest ways to look instantly put together with minimal effort. Even if you have nothing else on your face, a hint of lip color can lift your complexion. It also works as an accessory or finishing touch for even the simplest outfits.

According to recent reports, as we get older, lips naturally feel drier and lose volume. A good balm nourishes and comforts parched lips, but if you want more pigment, many lipsticks are designed for mature skin.

First, steer clear of ultra-matte formulas, as they tend to dehydrate lips and highlight every fine lip line imaginable. They also tend to look flat.

According to recent reports, for extra long wear, try a velvety, soft-matte formula instead. It delivers a similar, statement-making finish that's elegant while creating a pillowy, plush effect.

Sources indicate that satin formulas perform well, too. The gentle shine creates the illusion of healthier-looking lips, and it feels less drying throughout the day. That mentioned, brighter shades like reds and oranges can be a little messy to apply, so apply one layer, blend with a fingertip, and blot with a tissue. Repeat to build intensity. If feathering (when the color "bleeds" into fine lines around your lips) is an issue, a clear lip liner around the perimeter should create a barrier.

It's always best to get your skincare benefits from your lip balm, but nourishing plant oils and hydrating ingredients such as glycerin and hyaluronic acid in your lipstick will help maintain hydration as the day goes on.

It has been revealed that for makeup artist and Jones Road founder Bobbi Brown, there are no hard-and-fast rules—no matter your age. "It's about your style, what you feel most comfortable in," she tells Bazaar UK.

It has been revealed that if you're keen on neutral tones, remember that neutral doesn't mean beige. "Pay attention to what your natural lip color is. I have a slightly bluish-purple tone to my lips. You might have more of a pink tone. It's really great to find a lipstick that really looks like your lips, and the only way is to test it on your bottom lip," claims Brown, who notes that a great neutral should not wash you out.

Revered makeup artist Bobbi Brown is no stranger to creating iconic lipsticks. The Classic Lip has all the hallmarks of a modern formula: creamy, intensely hydrating, and richly pigmented. The 12-color range offers enough variety without overwhelming consumers. Expect skin-enhancing neutrals and bolder tones for any occasion.

In a recent development, trinny London excels at makeup for mature skin, and this recent launch is certainly no exception. It's a glossy, mega-hydrating formula that reflects light beautifully, making lips look plumper, and it's formulated with peptides to help reduce fine lines over time. There's a full spectrum of nude shades, but we love the bold red Poppy for festive nights.

In a recent development, A richly pigmented, buttery-smooth formula that promises to minimize dryness without sacrificing impact. It contains plenty of nourishing oils to keep moisture lasting without feathering into fine lines. It has a rosy scent, so keep that in mind if you're sensitive to fragrance.

It has been revealed that everything Victoria Beckham does delivers instant polish to the lips without extra effort. This slimline lipstick is no exception. It glides on like a tinted lip balm, adding a touch more color while infusing skin with hydration. VB has perfected the art of neutrals, so expect to find easy-to-wear hues for all skin tones. Glide on, then pat to blend any hard edges. It's one of those formulas you won't need a mirror to apply.

Refillable makeup isn't newly introduced, but Lisa Eldridge has painstakingly ensured every part of her Rouge Experience lipstick is recyclable, while it still looks like it belongs on a movie star's dresser. The lipstick formula combines oil, gel, and cream to ensure all-day comfort. The color pigments build easily and sit between a soft matte and a shiny finish. It's unfragranced, too.

In a recent development, creative and image director of Christian Dior Makeup, Peter Philips, reviewed Dior's bestselling lip colors worldwide to create a tightly curated collection of 10 sophisticated, wearable shades for every skin tone. Nude doesn't mean beige, according to Philips, and this line includes a complexion-lifting neutral, whatever that looks like to you. The emollient formula glides on like balmy, satin lipstick but won't budge once it sets. Expect long-wear color without the drying side effects.

In a recent development, when Hourglass creates matte lipsticks, rest assured they feature elevated colors and sit beautifully on the lips without highlighting fine lines, feathering, or flaking. This elegant formula feels velvety soft, with buildable pigments that stay put.

Sisley's interpretation of a shimmery, luminous lip color is as elevated as you've come to expect from this storied French brand. Phyto Rouge Shine is infused with the finest pearlescent particles in a translucent base, delivering sheer, buildable color and a plumping effect that still looks understated and grown-up.

Recent findings suggest that hermès Beauty creative director Gregoris Pyrpylis drew inspiration from Hermès scarves when designing this collection. This translates into buildable, luminous color and a smooth, tactile finish that feels like a second skin. Even the deepest shades look refined, with a radiance that brightens the face. Plus, the wide, angled bullet makes application as easy as wearing a lip balm.

Industry observers note that not all liquid lipsticks are created equal. Violette's soft, whipped texture is truly modern, delivering intense colors without a heavy feel. The gel-cream texture blurs out fine lines, too, so lips appear plush and smooth.

#134994. Latest Update: I Tested Peloton's Latest, More Affordable Folding Treadmill

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1687 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Gq ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: I Tested Peloton's Latest, More Affordable Folding Treadmill

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1687 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gq

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that in my mind and, I think the minds of many others, Peloton has always been a stationary bike brand.
  • Nevertheless, Peloton actually has been making treadmills since 2018.
  • The fresh Tread Flex, however, heads in a slightly different direction.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that in my mind and, I think the minds of many others, Peloton has always been a stationary bike brand. The Bike, after all, was its first product, turning the Peloton name into a catch-all term for at-home cycling that we now hear everywhere, from broadcasts of the Tour de France and Giro d'Italia to television sitcoms. (A running gag online is that Peloton's upscale, soothing video workout content is worlds away from The Office's Dwight Schrute leading a group of stationary riders off an imaginary cliff.).

Nevertheless, Peloton actually has been making treadmills since 2018. The first Tread delivered the same proposition as the Bike: premium hardware that looks good enough to bring out of the basement, as well as access to interactive, instructor-led runs and HIIT classes on a major, immersive screen. Over the years, Peloton has brought improvements to that first Tread: larger screens, voice controls, AI-informed movement tracking for form analysis and coaching.

The fresh Tread Flex, however, heads in a slightly different direction. It has a simpler belt, simpler speakers, a smaller screen. It's $1,300 cheaper than the next step up, and $4,500 cheaper (!) than Peloton's slat belt-equipped Tread+ Vision. Its affordability isn't even its main selling point, however, because the Tread Flex has a nifty final trick: it folds up to save space.

Could these space and money-saving tactics make the Tread as popular as the Bike? Well, I run nearly every day, and ever since a tester Tread Flex demonstrated up at my door, I've been doing it indoors much more frequently. In my experience, here's what makes Peloton's latest worth considering.

Sources indicate that treadmills tend to have a problem that stationary bikes don't: the nicer they get, the bigger they get. Premium models have larger motors and roomier running platforms. In short, they're heavy. (The Tread+ Vision is a hefty 460 pounds.) The Tread Flex is 170 pounds less, and that's crucial to its ability to fold up, because that feature wouldn't be much of a selling point if it felt like adding a power clean to the end of every run.

It has been revealed that in reality, stowing the Tread Flex is quite easy. You just lift up the running deck from the end and push it forward until a hydraulic cylinder locks into place. There's a pin clip to lock it. To drop it down, you push forward on the deck and then on the hydraulic support, then walk it back. At about 45 degrees, the hydraulics take over completely; you can go put on your running shoes while a gentle thump lets you know the deck is back on the ground.

Recent findings suggest that folding up the Tread Flex drops its area from about 16.5 square feet to half that. (The Tread+ Vision is around 19.25.) Just as importantly, I've discovered, is that lifting the deck brings the machine up onto a set of locking wheels. I've kept mine in a designated corner, but it's so easy to move that it wouldn't be much hassle to wheel it out and lower it for every workout, if your space required it. Get your cardio out of the way, then get your cardio out of the way.

Okay, so folding and moving a treadmill might be a pain if you're using it every day. But I suspect if you're running that often, you're doing some of it outside. I live less than an hour away from the Canadian border, and run on roads and trails five or six times a week all year round. Good layers get you pretty far, and there's a reason why run clubs continue to boom while SoulCycle-adjacent Mile High Run Club closed all its studios this year.

Sources indicate that treadmills are for something else. They're for a warm-up prior to lifting, or for bootcamp-style HIIT workouts that combine sprinting intervals with weight intervals. The prioritization value of time spent doing these doesn't seem to align with the space investment a treadmill requires if you don't have a pool house or major garage. (I have a sun porch-slash-mudroom where I keep firewood and ski boots in the winter and a napping couch in the summer.).

This is how, I think, the Tread Flex makes the ultimate proposition as the ideal home treadmill. A treadmill doesn't replace a usual running routine; it adds to it. On Monday I do my usual seven miles down the road and back on the river trails; on Tuesday I let Andy Speer kick my ass with sprints and kickstand deadlifts. (And, sure, when it's -10° and blowing in late January, I might run inside, now that I have the option.).

It has been revealed that none of the above would matter as much if it came at the cost of quality. I've run on hotel treadmills that sound like your grandma's washing machine and feel similar to how they look, i.e., stomping around on hollow plastic. The Tread Flex may not have the cushioned slat belt the Tread+ Vision has, but it's definitely not that.

In a recent development, what it does have is a spec that's right in line with top-notch treadmills. Its max speed is 12.5 miles per hour (a 4:48 mile, in runner's units), a 12.5% max incline grade (but no decline), and a 20-inch by 59-inch running surface that, though not cushioned, feels good to run on. The swiveling screen is nice and significant at 21.5 inches, with HD resolution and a touchscreen interface. I particularly like how adjusting speed and incline is done with rolling knobs, which feel much better—and more natural—to engage with than buttons when you're gasping at threshold pace.

On top of that is Peloton's interactive experience: You can take live classes where you can pit yourself against others and get kudos from the instructor. The pre-recorded catalogue includes thousands of classes for yoga, Pilates, and meditation, in addition to strength and the running, cycling, and rowing the firm makes machines for.

Sources indicate that the Tread Flex also provides personalized training plans, smart pacing guidance based on where you're at, automatically adjusting incline for classes, and of course leaderboards and an entire ecosystem of badges and achievements to earn, if you're into all that. For $50 per year, that is.

According to recent reports, oh, and did I mention it's a good-looking machine? It's sleek; an attractive, soft-edged Z with a minimal screen instead of a board of colorful buttons. Nobody's throwing around the word "console" to describe this thing. That's good; home gym setups deserve different consideration than gym rigs. If images of Crunch Fitness flash through your head every time you glance into the corner, something has missed the mark.

Where Peloton's Tread Vision treadmills are clearly high-end, the Tread Flex toes the line against mainstream consumer models. Its features match up with some of the most popular machines, and its price, while at the higher end of the spectrum, does too. But the Tread Flex gets there with more style, and with Peloton's huge ecosystem of live and archived class content.

So, if we're looking at other treadmills out there, my quick answer is yes. The Tread Flex is the utilitarian Peloton Treadmill, but it's still a Peloton treadmill.

Recent findings suggest that how you answer this question really requires asking yourself a series of other questions first. What do you want a treadmill for? How much do you want to invest? Do you want access to fitness classes—especially ones other than running—and are you okay with the $50/month subscription fee?

Form factor and access to classes and content are non-negotiables. The Tread Flex might be Peloton's upcoming entry-level treadmill, but it's far from a simple running machine. Flex refers to that nifty fold-up feature, but also to this treadmill's ability to integrate into an exercise program that also includes strength training, HIIT workouts, yoga, and on and on.

Sources indicate that as a runner who prefers to log miles outside whenever possible, I was encouraged by how much I enjoyed running on the Tread Flex. The classes are fun, and Peloton's instructors are real pros, but even in Just Run mode, the Tread Flex proved responsive and comfy. It's getting dark around 4:30 PM these days, and my daylight windows for running on the well-used roads around me have narrowed like a Death Star trash compactor. It's nice to know I can snag seven miles after sundown if need be.

Sources indicate that well, if you aren't limited by space or cash, the Tread Vision and Tread+ Vision get you bigger screens, AI-enabled running form feedback and coaching, and a more cushioned, broader running area. If you just prefer running or walking on a treadmill to doing it outside, investing more heavily in a treadmill is worth considering (though the Tread Flex will still be great).

Industry observers note that the Tread Flex's real competition is the NordicTrack Commercial 1750, which you'll find recommended on just about every treadmill buying guide on the internet. The machines are similar in function and specs, but there are some differences. The NordicTrack's running surface is two inches wider and one inch longer; it has a slightly more powerful motor; it can decline to -3% grade; its belt is slightly cushioned; it has a built-in fan; and NordicTrack's class and entertainment platform, iFit, is cheaper at $39 a month.

In comparison, the Tread Flex takes up slightly less space, has a higher max speed (12.5 mph over 12 mph), a steeper incline (12.5% over 12%), and a larger screen (21.5 inches over 16 inches). The rolling knobs to adjust speed and incline are nicer to use. My partner, who designs commercial and residential interior spaces, agrees with me that the Tread Flex is a better-looking machine.

Recent findings suggest that list price for the Tread Flex is $300 cheaper, but the NordicTrack seems to be perpetually on sale. So it might come down to looks, that 3% decline, or what class platform you'd like to buy into.

Olivia Colman debuted a sophisticated hair transformation Monday night at the premiere of Only Murders in London.

Celebrating the sixth season of the Disney+ show, in which she guest-stars alongside Steve Martin and Selena Gomez, Colman wore head-to-toe Celine, walking the red carpet in a striking silk cape top, tailored trousers, and pointed boots.

It has been revealed that equally elegant was the Oscar-winning actress’s latest hair color, her second in as many months. Earlier this autumn, Colman debuted a polished “smoky steel” hue; however, she stepped out in the capital this week with an inky black shade.

Hairstylist Earl Simms created Colman’s new look, and the actress joins a handful of other celebrities embracing dark, moody tones this winter. This month alone, Dakota Johnson was seen sporting fresh, jet-black hair, while Billie Piper and Hailey Bieber have also gone considerably darker in recent weeks.

As the nights draw in and summer becomes but a distant memory, many stylish women opt for deep, cozy hues at salon appointments, and while dark brunette shades are generally lower maintenance than bright blondes, there are still a few housekeeping rules, as Luci Green, a colorist at London salon Larry King Hair, previously told Bazaar.

While brunettes might need less frequent touch-ups than blondes, any chemically colored hair still needs care and attention. “The best way to treat freshly coloured hair at home is to always use a professional color protect shampoo and conditioner,” Green explained. “It’s also important to avoid using too much heat,” she added.

Sources indicate that but first things first: Always get a consultation. Green shared: “I’d always advise having a consultation with a colorist before any color change, so they can work out what the best shade is for your skin tone.” Noted!

Industry News: What Is Smart Aging? Experts Explain the Skin Care Shift Replacing Antiaging

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1545 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Elle

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor.
  • Sources indicate that beauty terminology has evolved quite rapidly in recent years—particularly around aging.
  • Natalia Guzman, FNP-C, CANS, a board-certified nurse practitioner at Atelier Aesthetix in Beverly Hills, explains that smart aging is a proactive, science-based approach to maintaining healthy, youthful-looking skin while embracing the natural aging process.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Sources indicate that beauty terminology has evolved quite rapidly in recent years—particularly around aging. What was long labeled antiaging has shifted toward more realistic definitions of what happens to skin and the body as we get older. But the latest buzzword, longevity, as ubiquitous as it’s become, doesn’t exactly fill the gap for those seeking ways to keep skin, hair, and the body looking youthful. Hailey Bieber’s recent use of the term “smart aging” just may be the word substitute the category has been missing.

Natalia Guzman, FNP-C, CANS, a board-certified nurse practitioner at Atelier Aesthetix in Beverly Hills, explains that smart aging is a proactive, science-based approach to maintaining healthy, youthful-looking skin while embracing the natural aging process. “Rather than trying to ‘stop’ aging altogether, which is biologically impossible, smart aging focuses on understanding how our skin changes over time and making informed decisions to preserve a healthy, strong, overall youthful appearance,” Guzman tells ELLE.

From a dermatologic perspective, Dr. Brianna Olamiju, a board-certified dermatologist with Spring Street Dermatology in NYC, offers this explanation: “Smart aging is about being proactive, making informed skin care choices, and supporting the skin’s natural functions over time. It involves protecting the skin from environmental damage, maintaining a healthy skin barrier, stimulating collagen production when appropriate, and addressing concerns such as fine lines, wrinkles, uneven pigmentation, and loss of elasticity,” says Olamiju. Ultimately, she says, smart aging is about helping your skin look and feel its best at every stage of life while embracing the natural aging process.

Guzman emphasizes that aging beautifully isn’t about looking young. “It’s about looking and feeling like the best version of yourself at every stage of life.”.

In a recent development, as skin evolves, collagen production gradually declines, cellular turnover slows, and environmental factors such as UV exposure, pollution, and lifestyle habits contribute to visible signs of aging. Guzman adds that smart aging means addressing these changes strategically through preventative skin care, healthy lifestyle choices, and, when appropriate, evidence-based aesthetic treatments. “I like to think of smart aging as investing in your skin’s future and being proactive rather than waiting until significant changes occur and attempting to reverse them,” Guzman says. “A lot of the time, the latter takes much more work, and sometimes it cannot be completely corrected.”.

According to Guzman, the biggest difference between smart aging and traditional antiaging is the philosophy behind it. “For decades, the beauty industry has promoted the idea that aging is something we need to fight, prevent, or erase,” notes Guzman. The term “antiaging” often focuses on correcting visible signs of aging, such as wrinkles, volume loss, pigmentation, and skin laxity.

In a recent development, both Guzman and Olamiju agree that smart aging takes a more holistic, comprehensive, and realistic approach. Olamiju indicates that anti-aging creates the expectation that we should try to look younger indefinitely. “Smart aging shifts the focus toward skin health, prevention, and maintaining long-term skin quality. Rather than viewing wrinkles, fine lines, and changes in skin textureas something that must be eliminated, smart aging encourages us to support the skin as it naturally evolves. It is less about fighting aging and more about aging well,” she explains. This approach, she adds, also emphasizes consistency, prevention, and individualized treatments rather than chasing every fresh product or cosmetic trend.

According to recent reports, guzman adds that smart aging, instead of fighting age, means working with the skin’s biology to help it function and look its best for as long as possible. “The main difference is that we’re not simply chasing wrinkles. We're creating a long-term strategy that prioritizes skin quality, natural-looking results, and overall skin health,” Guzman emphasizes. “To me, anti-aging is often about correcting what we see today, while smart aging is about preventing and protecting what we’ll see tomorrow.”.

Olamiju and Guzman are completely aligned on the first step in a smart aging routine: wearing sunscreen daily. “The foundation of smart aging starts with a consistent skincare routine and healthy lifestyle habits. Daily broad-spectrum sunscreen with an SPF of at least 30 is arguably the most important step because ultraviolet exposure is one of the leading contributors to premature skin aging, including wrinkles, loss of elasticity, and uneven pigmentation,” states Olamiju. Guzman adds that UV exposure contributes significantly to collagen breakdown and changes in skin texture, noting that sunscreen is essential even on cloudy days.

Olamiju also recommends incorporating topical antioxidants, such as vitamin C, to help protect against environmental oxidative stress, along with moisturizers containing ingredients like ceramides and hyaluronic acid to support hydration and the skin barrier. “Retinoids, including retinol and prescription tretinoin, can be beneficial for improving fine lines, skin texture, and collagen production, provided they are appropriate for the individual,” Olamiju describes.

Dermalogica AGE Smart Biolumin-C Serum.

Sunday Riley Ceramor Ceramide Barrier Replenishing Cream.

SkinMedica Retinol Complex 0.5 Serum.

Bio-Therapeutic bt-sculpt Gen2 Microcurrent Facial Sculpting System.

According to recent reports, once your at-home routine is in place, Guzman recommends strategically incorporating preventive and corrective aesthetic treatments. “Depending on the patient’s age, anatomy, and concerns, treatments such as neuromodulators, collagen-stimulating injectables, microneedling, and energy-based devices may help maintain or improve certain aspects of skin appearance,” claims Guzman. The key, she adds, is choosing the right treatment for the right patient rather than following every new aesthetic trend. Olamiju includes chemical peels in a very similar list of in-office treatments, depending, of course, on an individual’s concerns, skin type, and goals.

Industry observers note that finally, the experts agree: don’t underestimate lifestyle. Adequate sleep, regular exercise, balanced nutrition rich in antioxidants and healthy fats, avoiding smoking, managing chronic stress, and limiting excessive alcohol consumption all contribute to overall health and can influence how our skin looks and functions.

The best time to start is earlier than most people think, Olamiju shares. Ideally in your 20s, when prevention can have a meaningful long-term impact. “This does not mean that someone in their 20s needs an elaborate skincare routine or aggressive cosmetic treatments. Rather, it is an opportunity to establish healthy habits, including daily sunscreen use, gentle cleansing, and consistent moisturizing,” indicates Olamiju.

Guzman advises starting a smart aging routine before you feel like you need to correct something, but it’s also never too late to begin. “I encourage patients to think of smart aging as something that evolves with them rather than a routine that begins at a specific birthday,” she adds, offering this decade-by-decade breakdown:.

Sources indicate that in your 20s. The priority should be prevention. This means establishing healthy skincare habits, wearing sunscreen consistently, maintaining hydration, and introducing targeted active ingredients when appropriate. At this stage, the goal isn’t to aggressively treat aging. It's to protect the skin and build a strong foundation.

In your 30s. You may begin noticing subtle changes in skin texture, fine lines, pigmentation, or elasticity. This is often a good time to reassess your skin care routine and consider professional treatments based on individual needs. It may also be time to consider a little Botox, energy-based treatments, and biostimulators, all depending on the individual’s needs.

In your 40s and 50s. Changes in collagen, facial volume, skin elasticity, and hormonal influences may become more noticeable. A smart aging approach at this stage may include a combination of medical-grade skin care, collagen-supporting treatments, and continued careful selection of aesthetic procedures.

In your 60s and beyond. The focus remains on maintaining skin health, supporting the skin barrier, addressing concerns such as dryness and uneven pigmentation, and choosing treatments that respect the skin’s changing needs.

Olamiju adds that even patients who begin prioritizing their skin health later in life can benefit significantly from consistent sun protection and an appropriately tailored skin care regimen.

In a recent development, guzman indicates this is one of the most vital conversations we should be having in modern aesthetics. Both experts say smart aging is not a one-size-fits-all concept. They explain that different skin types and skin tones can experience visible aging differently, and understanding those differences is essential to creating a safe and effective treatment plan.

Sources indicate that individuals with lighter skin tones may notice fine lines, redness, and visible sun damage earlier, particularly if they have a history of significant UV exposure. Those with darker skin tones may have more visible concerns related to uneven pigmentation, post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, and changesin skin tone. “Melanin provides some natural protection against ultraviolet radiation, but it does not eliminate the risk of sun damage or skin cancer, so daily sunscreen remains essential for all skin tones,” Olamiju warns.

Guzman adds that these pigmentation concerns also become especially crucial when we introduce aesthetic treatments such as lasers, chemical peels, or microneedling. “Certain procedures and treatment settings carry a greater risk of pigmentation changes in patients with more melanin-rich skin, so proper patient selection, device choice, and clinical expertise are critical,” Guzman notes.

Overall, smart aging should combine science, prevention, consistency, and thoughtful aesthetic care. “Aging is inevitable. How we care for ourselves throughout that process is where we have the opportunity to make a meaningful difference,” Guzman concludes.

My holidays were split between regions growing up. We spent Thanksgiving at my dad’s side, and Christmas with my mom’s. According to recent reports, what makes a Midwest Thanksgiving, you may ask? All of the classics are present, plus a few surprising favorites that, in my house, no holiday is complete without. We think beyond the turkey, sometimes skip mashed potatoes for a cheesy casserole, and have to be careful not to fill up on all the rolls (butter and honey better be on the table). Ready to celebrate Midwest-style? Here are some recipes that your holiday won’t be complete without:.

Made with canned pineapple, pistachio pudding, and Cool Whip, this retro crowd-pleasing dessert “salad” will take you straight back to the ’70s with just one bite. It’s the perfect recipe to throw together if you don’t have a ton of time, but you need to take something to that potluck or family gathering.

Thanksgiving is equally about food and football, so this tailgate-inspired stuffing is a no-brainer. Filled with beer cheese sauce and topped with crispy bacon, this twist on the classic holiday side is so irresistible, it’ll be gone long before halftime of that first Thanksgiving Day game.

Pepper Jelly & Cream Cheese Bites.

In a recent development, it takes less than than 5 minutes to pour some pepper jelly over cream cheese and place some crackers around. These bites are slightly more elevated without many more steps. Recent findings suggest that don't be fooled by the name—the only thing deathly about this casserole is how absolutely delicious it is. This cheesy, creamy casserole is a staple at every holiday in my Kansas home, and Thanksgiving is no exception. Yes, we often have mashed potatoes too.

According to recent reports, for this recipe, we ditched canned cream of mushroom soup and went for fresh instead. Cook the mushrooms enough that they get a little caramelized, and you'll really be good to go.

The pretzel crust proves to be an ideal complement to the rich cream cheese layer and the sweet strawberries with their Jell-O glaze.

Industry observers note that turkey usually rules the roost at Thanksgiving, but it's not the only centerpiece present at many Midwestern holiday tables. Depending on how many family members are coming, my family has been known to prepare a turkey and a ham—it's the best of both worlds!

A cheese ball is peak party appetizer nostalgia, and these cheese ball bites are here to put a fresh, shareable twist on the classic. They’re so simple to make, only require a handful of ingredients, and are super versatile based on what you have on hand.

I'll clarify that when I say stuffing, I'm actually referring to dressing. Forget Plymouth Rock This Thanksgiving. American History Is Better Reflected by a Different Stone.

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (852 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Esquire

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Let me send out a little Thanksgiving advice to potential tourists planning to visit us in the Commonwealth (God save it!) in the future.
  • Sources indicate that first of all, Plymouth Rock is a boulder in a hole in the ground.
  • Even Alexis de Tocqueville, America’s greatest tourist and, therefore, its primordial sucker, fell for the Rock’s charisma.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Let me send out a little Thanksgiving advice to potential tourists planning to visit us in the Commonwealth (God save it!) in the future. If some local tells you to go to see Plymouth Rock, tell them you have tickets for a four-day Duck Tour of the Freedom Trail. I promise you: Seeing Paul Revere’s house four times is infinitely more interesting than seeing Plymouth Rock once.

Sources indicate that first of all, Plymouth Rock is a boulder in a hole in the ground. Oh, there’s a classical templish thing above it, but it’s still a boulder in a hole in the ground. Second, there’s almost no historical evidence that any pilgrim feet ever trod upon the rock in question. None of the contemporaneous accounts mention it. It was a nonagenarian named Thomas Faunce who, in 1741, 121 years after the Mayflower arrived, decided that this was the rock on which all the Bradfords and their shipmates disembarked. It moved around Plymouth a lot in the early years. In 1774, it cracked in two, which some folks took as an ill omen for the burgeoning Revolution. (Pieces of it are in the Smithsonian) The year 1620 was carved into the boulder’s surface in 1880. In 1920, it found its permanent home. In 1990, writing in The Newly introduced Yorker, John McPhee wrote of the rock:.

Even Alexis de Tocqueville, America’s greatest tourist and, therefore, its primordial sucker, fell for the Rock’s charisma.

Damn, Alexis. Have some Madeira and chillez out, mon ami.

If you want to see a genuinely interesting boulder, drive 42 minutes west to the town of Berkley, where you will find Dighton Rock State Park. In another templish building, there is Dighton Rock. It is a six-sided, five-foot-high slab of sandstone. It is also adorned with ancient petroglyphic carvings of uncertain origin. There are depictions of animals and an assortment of lines and whorls and mysterious designs. In 1680, John Danforth got a look at the Dighton Rock and not even his recently bestowed Harvard degree could explain them. He made drawings of the carvings he could see. (At the time Danforth saw it, the rock was partially submerged in the Taunton River.) It also drew the interest of local celebrities like Cotton Mather and poet James Russell Lowell.

Danforth’s opinion was that the carvings were made by the local Native tribes, and he thought it depicted an ancient battle of some sort. (If there’s anything like a consensus among people who have studied the carvings, it’s Danforth’s.) However logical that might seem, it didn’t tamp down speculation as the years went by. Down through the centuries, the carvings have been attributed to Phoenicians, Carthaginians, Vikings, Portuguese adventurers, Chinese explorers, and Japanese mariners. And, of course, inevitably … aliens.

It has been revealed that however, it was a professor of psychology from Brown University who had the right of it, I think. Edmund Delabarre was a well-respected psychological researcher in the first half of the 20th century. He also grew fascinated with the study of rock carvings in and around Narragansett Bay. Ultimately, his researches brought him to the shores of the Taunton River and to the Dighton Rock.

Ultimately, Delabarre dismissed all the other claims of origin and concluded that the carvings on the Dighton Rock were probably made by a crew sailing under the command of one Miguel Corte-Real, a Portuguese explorer who charted about 600 miles of coastline in and around the Canadian Maritimes. In 1502, Corte-Real set sail for the western Atlantic, seeking to discover what had become of his brother, Gaspar, who had not returned from a voyage to Newfoundland. Miguel vanished, too.

Delabarre’s contention was that Miguel had made it to New England, and he argued that the inscription was a form of abbreviated Latin that proclaimed Corte-Real to be “king of the Indians.” In his 2017 book The Place of Stone, Douglas Hunter pretty much demolished all of the outre interpretations of the carvings, arguing that the carvings were of Native origin, and that the other interpretations were elements in the erasure of Native history and the legacy of bloody colonization, of which, ironically, the settlement at Plymouth was Ground Zero. The people who didn’t step onshore on a rock in Plymouth debuted one of the first campaigns of the greater American genocide. As Hunter wrote:.

Recent findings suggest that so there’s American history on the Thanksgiving of 2026, ground up between two stones, one a legend with a counterfeit past, and another a mystery with a stolen past. The latter is by far the more compelling. Its history encompasses all of the history, good and bad, of this appropriated continent. Edmund Delabarre was wrong about Miguel Corte-Real and the Portuguese, but he might have been more right than he knew when he wrote that Dighton Rock was a kind of test. In the ambiguity of its carvings at the time of Delabarre’s work, a person saw in them what he wanted to see. Not all of it was pretty, or ennobling, or triumphal. But it's all ours.

Thankfully, Omega and Swatch Aren’t Done Making Snoopy MoonSwatches

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that four-plus years into the massive collaboration between Omega and Swatch, the partners are still finding ways to reimagine their blockbuster MoonSwatch.
  • According to recent reports, meet the fresh Mission to Earthphase - Silver Snowflake.
  • It has been revealed that the black-on-black-on-black design works to great effect here.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that four-plus years into the massive collaboration between Omega and Swatch, the partners are still finding ways to reimagine their blockbuster MoonSwatch. And despite nearly 40 iterations of the piece, they still generate massive excitement. The most recent version required interested collectors to fill out an “Electronic Swatch Timepiece Application” in hopes of being selected to purchase one. More than 1.2 million people happily played along. Now, Swatch and Omega are back and playing the hits with a Snoopy-inflected version of the MoonSwatch.

According to recent reports, meet the fresh Mission to Earthphase - Silver Snowflake. The blacked-out watch is reminiscent of the collector-favorite Speedmaster known as the “Dark Side of the Moon” from 2013. What that watch was lacking compared to this one is an adorable drawing of Snoopy and Woodstock dressed as astronauts and a special silver disc with a unique laser-engraved snowflake design. Safe to say, Omega and Swatch have another hit on their hands.

It has been revealed that the black-on-black-on-black design works to great effect here. Everything is rendered in the dark shade: the case, bezel, dial, and matching rubber strap with Velcro closure. Like all MoonSwatch references, the Silver Snowflake model measures 42mm in diameter and features the asymmetric design familiar to Speedy lovers everywhere.

But it’s the easter eggs on the dial that really make this MoonSwatch stand out. Naturally, there are several hidden details. For instance, check out the miniature skis standing in for the indices at 11 o'clock. That’s a special shoutout to the Apollo 11 50th Anniversary of the Speedmaster. This model also returns to a trick employed by the “Cold Moon” MoonSwatch released last November. That watch and this one feature a snowflake design generated at random, meaning each watch is functionally unique. Here, the snowflake appears on a silver-coated disc in the moonphase complication at 2 o’clock.

At 10 o’clock is Swatch and Omega’s signature MoonSwatch “Earth phase” indicator, which bears an image of the Earth with UV ink-coated oceans set against a starry background. Again, look closely: Switzerland is represented in white, its UV ink glowing green in the dark, while Snoopy and Woodstock, represented below, feature secret details in blue-emission UV ink. Protecting the dial is a box-shaped, bio-sourced crystal with an engraved “S” in the center—a detail familiar to fans of vintage Speedmasters, some of which bore “O”-engraved Hesalite crystals.

Sources indicate that like several other MoonSwatch models in the brand’s now-vast collection, buying the Mission to Earthphase - Silver Snowflake requires navigating certain arcane rules. The first part is simple: it’ll be available in stores worldwide this Black Friday, November 27th. However, following that, your only chance to nab one will be when it’s snowing in Switzerland. (And only until March 20th, 2027.) When it comes to the MoonSwatch, simply buying one has become half the fun.

Industry News: Alex Prager Has Hollywood Dreams

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (711 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Elle

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that alex Prager was in her cubicle at an internet startup, staring at the endless rows of other desks, when she realized that something was terribly wrong.
  • It didn’t take long for Prager to start getting noticed in art circles.
  • It has been revealed that prager’s color-saturated works capture cinematic scenes that bring to mind classic Hitchcock films.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that alex Prager was in her cubicle at an internet startup, staring at the endless rows of other desks, when she realized that something was terribly wrong. “The rest of my life flashed in my mind,” she says. She began to cry. “It was like that Talking Heads song: And you may find yourself in a beautiful house / With a beautiful wife / And you may ask yourself, / ‘Well…how did I get here?’” she says. “This was not my life.” Soon after, she attended a show of William Eggleston’s work and left certain that her future was in photography. Within a week, she’d bought a used Nikon N90s camera and darkroom equipment. “I just knew, the way that you know you have a face and you know who you love. I knew from that moment forward what my path was,” she says.

It didn’t take long for Prager to start getting noticed in art circles. And this winter will be one of the most significant seasons of her career, with both a major solo museum show at the Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art in Bentonville, Arkansas, and an exhibition at the Fresh York gallery Lehmann Maupin. DreamQuil, her first feature film, was released in theaters this fall and will be available to stream in December.

It has been revealed that prager’s color-saturated works capture cinematic scenes that bring to mind classic Hitchcock films. She creates full worlds for her photos, with sets, casts, and impeccable period costumes. Her pieces gained notice with her 2007 show “Polyester” at L.A.’s Robert Berman Gallery. The series revealed women, perfectly attired in ’60s-era looks, posed in evocative ways. A heavily made-up girl clutches a Massive Gulp, a flaxen braid thrown over one shoulder; four young women huddle together in swimsuits, a plane flying across the perfect blue sky above. An ominous feeling pervades.

Industry observers note that her work sparkles on the surface but explores something darker underneath. “The first color photograph I took was staged and a play on The Wizard of Oz and death, but it was very colorful and beautiful. I was interested in the way to explore something that felt layered. Underneath it, you find there are very uncomfortable things or darker stories and emotions,” Prager explains.

According to recent reports, prager steadily built up a following through a series of gallery demonstrates, but things changed markedly in 2010 when her work was selected to be shown in the elite “New Photography” exhibit at MoMA. She had her first solo show at the Corcoran Gallery of Art in Washington, D.C., three years later. She’s also done work for magazines and brands like Cartier, Disney, and Apple.

According to recent reports, “My work has always been about my personal challenges and things that I’m not really understanding in the world, but I think more and more it becomes less about me and my emotions. That’s probably also me becoming a mother and growing up, but the world has changed,” states Prager, whose son Francis is 9. The scale of her work has grown—bigger audiences, more ambitious concepts, a greater ability to stage elaborate photography—but the approach hasn’t. It’s still about the questions she needs answers to.

The idea for DreamQuil came to Prager during the pandemic (she was inspired by a meme that advertised YearQuil, a fictitious product that would allow people to sleep through the misery of 2020), and she wrote the script with her sister, Vanessa Prager. Elizabeth Banks stars as a woman who’s living in a depressing future world where people rarely leave their homes and finds herself dealing with her robot clone.

Opening two major reveals within months of the release of her film wasn’t something Prager anticipated—each alone would have been a high point in her career—but she often does her best work amid a frenzy of activity. “I thrive in a bit of chaos,” she says. “I like to try to mold it and wrestle with it and attempt to control it and bend it to my will. It doesn’t always happen exactly the way I want, but it infuses me with inspiration and energy.”.

This story appears in the December 2026/January 2027 issue of ELLE.

Popeyes Beat KFC In My Chicken Sandwich Showdown—But Can It Take Down Chick-fil-A?

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, few fast food rivalries are as competitive as the battle for the best chicken sandwich.
  • Industry observers note that in my previous chicken sandwich showdown, I put KFC and Popeyes head-to-head to see which chain served the better sandwich.
  • Recent findings suggest that chick-fil-A has built its reputation around a simple, flavorful chicken sandwich that doesn’t need much to stand out.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, few fast food rivalries are as competitive as the battle for the best chicken sandwich. And while plenty of chains have introduced their own versions over the years, Chick-fil-A and Popeyes remain two of the biggest names in the conversation.

Industry observers note that in my previous chicken sandwich showdown, I put KFC and Popeyes head-to-head to see which chain served the better sandwich. Popeyes ultimately came out on top, thanks to its bold seasoning, crispy breading, and well-balanced toppings. This time, I’m putting Popeyes up against one of its biggest competitors: Chick-fil-A.

Recent findings suggest that chick-fil-A has built its reputation around a simple, flavorful chicken sandwich that doesn’t need much to stand out. Popeyes, meanwhile, practically broke the internet when it introduced its now-famous chicken sandwich in 2019, sparking a fast food frenzy.

According to recent reports, I ordered each chain’s original chicken sandwich to compare flavor, texture, juiciness, and overall balance. Both have their strengths, but only one can move on as my favorite.

Chick-fil-A’s Original Chicken Sandwich keeps things simple with a breaded chicken fillet, pickles, and a toasted bun.

In a recent development, chick-fil-A’s chicken is so recognizable for a reason. The seasoning and brine give the fillet a savory, slightly tangy flavor that’s hard to beat, while the crispy breading contrasts nicely with the juicy chicken. The pickles also do their job, adding just enough acidity and crunch to balance out the richness.

According to recent reports, my biggest complaint is that I wanted a little more from the sandwich. Compared to other fast food chicken sandwiches I’ve tried, many of which come with some type of sauce, Chick-fil-A’s original feels a bit plain. The chicken has enough flavor to stand on its own, but I think a little mayo or another sauce would have made the overall sandwich even better.

Still, there’s something to be mentioned for a chicken sandwich that relies almost entirely on the quality and flavor of the chicken itself.

In a recent development, popeyes’ Classic Chicken Sandwich features a breaded chicken fillet, pickles, mayo, and a toasted brioche bun. The sandwich that practically broke the internet when it launched in 2019 still lives up to the hype.

Industry observers note that I’ve had this sandwich before where the chicken was slightly dry in spots, but thankfully that wasn’t the case this time. The fillet was juicy, flavorful, and incredibly well-seasoned. The breading had a satisfying crunch, and the bold, savory flavor made me want to keep going back for another bite.

Sources indicate that the mayo was another vital part of the sandwich, adding a tangy creaminess that complemented the chicken without overpowering it. Paired with the crisp pickles, it helped balance out the richness of the fried fillet.

It has been revealed that I also really appreciated the proportions. The soft brioche bun held everything together without overwhelming the chicken, and each bite had a good balance of meat, breading, sauce, and pickles.

According to recent reports, while Popeyes might not always deliver the most consistently juicy chicken, everything came together particularly well during this taste test. Between the seasoning, crispy breading, and well-balanced toppings, it’s easy to understand why this sandwich became such a phenomenon in the first place.

Popeyes already managed to beat KFC in my previous comparison, and after going up against Chick-fil-A, it’s keeping its winning streak alive.

Sources indicate that chick-fil-A arguably has the more distinctive chicken flavor, thanks to its savory, slightly tangy seasoning. But when I’m ordering a chicken sandwich, I want the entire thing to work together, and that’s where Popeyes has the advantage.

Chick-fil-A is still a great option, especially if you prefer a simpler sandwich that lets the chicken do most of the work. But after trying both, Popeyes delivered the better overall experience. With two wins under its belt, Popeyes is proving to be a pretty tough sandwich to beat.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that bobbi Althoff has a baby face and a vocal fry.
  • It has been revealed that we’ve known each other for 20 minutes.
  • Industry observers note that it’s an essay entitled “I Hate Myself,” written by Althoff when she was a teenager mired in a bout of depression and anxiety made worse by bullies at school.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that bobbi Althoff has a baby face and a vocal fry. Her tenor––which you’ve likely encountered in your TikTok feed, whether or not you know her name––is vaguely baritone and sharply deadpan, an oddly melodic gravel on the eardrum. Depending on who you ask, it’s either endearing, or lazy, or simply slutty. Despite rising to fame on a skittish gaze, the 29-year-old MomTokker turned podcaster turned non-Mormon cast member of Secret Lives of Mormon Wives is now holding eye contact.

It has been revealed that we’ve known each other for 20 minutes. She puts down her fork and palms her phone. She wants to read me something, she says, her gemstone-encrusted ring (reading “MOM”) catching the sunlight streaming into The Dominick hotel, where Althoff is staying during the unseasonably warm week of the Mormon Wives premiere.

Industry observers note that it’s an essay entitled “I Hate Myself,” written by Althoff when she was a teenager mired in a bout of depression and anxiety made worse by bullies at school. I’d asked what she would title her memoir, if she were to write one, and how she handles online hate, from being accused of sleeping with Drake after interviewing him for her podcast to rumors that her marriage ended due to infidelity to scrutiny about her appearance. “Can a girl gain some weight in her face without you guys fucking saying she has cheek filler?” she wrote on Instagram. “Can a girl be insecure about her upper lip and get some fucking lip filler without you guys fucking commenting on it?” Althoff has been at the center of myriad social media firestorms, some motored by straightforward, internet-enabled misogyny and others by exasperation with her indirect, vaguely hostile approach to engaging with her podcast guests.

It has been revealed that she takes a breath, and begins reading. “I want so badly to be able to show everyone the real me, the person that is hurt and is scared to trust anyone, the little girl that is funny, loud, and doesn't care what other people think. Instead of being myself, I create a different personality to satisfy everyone's needs. I hide the real me behind fake smiles and high-pitched laughs.” She pauses, then chuckles (at a normal pitch).

Recent findings suggest that “I was 14 when I wrote that,” she continues. “And that was before ChatGPT. I wrote that myself.”.

According to recent reports, A smattering of the many awkward—or awkwardly flirtatious—and reliably fury-baiting encounters that have gone down on Althoff’s The Really Good Podcast since its inception in 2023: She and Jason DeRulo LARP a date that gets interrupted by an attempted larceny. While next to him in bed, she informs Drake that Aubrey is a girl’s name. She accuses Michael Cera of founding Cerave, then argues with him about whether his wife needs to know that their feet touched. Lil Yachty threatens to teach her to dance. An oral mishap cum Freudian slip—did she say magician or musician?—in a conversation with Sukihana appears to spark a feud, but instead jumpstarts a friendship and another podcast, this year’s surprisingly raw and affectionate That’s BS with Bobbi and Suki.

Despite her reputation as an invulnerable, even defensive interlocutor, Althoff is strikingly invested in self-exposure. She has spoken openly about her severe struggles with mental illness, insecurities around beauty, her plans to get breast implants, and her painful experience with botched Botox injections. Her penchant for oversharing, she told me, startles her interview subjects, inspiring their own surprising and frank disclosures in return.

Recent findings suggest that “I’m like, hi, nice to meet you, I tried to kill myself,” she tells me. From a young age, she has used comedy to cope with the indignities of womanhood, and she comes by her wry, bluntly charming humor honestly. “Mom, by the time you read this, I’m going to be chilling with Satan,” she remembers writing in a note she left for her mother as a teenager when, she tells me, she attempted suicide. “Keep in mind, I literally was so religious that I accepted that I was going to go to hell for killing myself.” Althoff grew up in a hyper-religious Christian household in California, where she was taught to believe in a classic set piece of Hell that involved “being burned alive forever.”.

Recent findings suggest that althoff has since left the Church, and with it the “conservative worldview” that characterized her adolescence and early adulthood, leading her to get married at the age of 22. Now, she claims, she is effortfully de-centering men after “being told that my purpose in life was to be a wife.” Which brings us to her latest venture: divorced, un-religious, founding cast member on a reality show that purports to follow a cabal of Mormon wives living in Orange County. Althoff says her friendships with fellow cast members have been formative and healing, her first experiences with genuine connection among a group of girls after a childhood defined by bullying and a young adulthood spent slaloming down social media slopes riddled with misogynistic vitriol that came from women just as often as it did men.

With her star turn as one of two non-Mormon, unmarried cast members in Mormon Wives, Althoff says she is she surrendering the control over her image that comes with having her own editing team for her podcast, which entails being “completely myself” to a “terrifying” degree. Where the original iteration of Mormon Wives, set in Salt Lake City, centered a pre-existing friend group, the OC spinoff opens on a cast of highly competitive loose acquaintances largely connected by a rabid desire to build their individual audiences. Entering the arena as the most random cast member makes watching Althoff build actual friendships in real-time bizarrely affecting. Instead of sitting safely in the interviewer’s chair, coquettishly crossing her legs and batting her eyelashes, this time those eyelashes are drenched in tears, and she’s not hiding the streaks of mascara dripping down her cheeks.

Recent findings suggest that those cheeks were once pumped full of Botox, which caused serious facial paralysis (a relatively rare side effect). But enduring a period in which she “couldn’t smile” inspired a shift in her approach to beauty standards and an appreciation for human foibles over cosmetic perfection. “I have been trying to find beauty in the fact that I’m not perfect,” she tells me. “Do I not like my cellulite? Yes, but, I can show it and it’s fine because I’m human. My boobs are saggy: I literally breastfed both of my kids.” Doing reality television also led to an epiphany: she’s been too hard on herself about her appearance. This occurred to her watching the show back with her new castmates-turned-friends, women who she finds beautiful. “I actually don’t need all this stuff,” she notes. “I don’t need to have a perfectly chiseled nose and perfect boobs.”.

Some might wonder whether joining the Mormon Wives cast, comprised largely of buxom, blonde, traditionally attractive women who in previous iterations of the show have attended group Botox appointments as a form of socializing, might be a counterintuitive way of deprogramming conservative aesthetic norms. But Mormon Wives runs on the tension inherent in its premise: these are women famous for being religious tradwives, who repeatedly slip and fall into subverting tradition: they are breadwinners, they are in bisexual throuples, they talk about sex on camera (even if they insist they only engage in it in the marriage bed). Perhaps most poignantly, they seem to find more emotional sustenance in their relationships with each other than any of their largely deadbeat, cheating, whining, soda-chugging boyfriends and husbands.

In the show’s premiere, she corrects an offscreen producer who calls her an influencer––she’s an internet personality. Online, she is disembodied, cut into clips, context-free and content-forward. And like many of today’s hyper-contemporary internet personalities, Althoff is paradoxically very famous and utterly unknown. As in: she has almost four million followers on Instagram, and every straight man I mentioned this profile to immediately had multiple, highly specific inquiries about interactions she’s had with male celebrities. (“What was it like to share a bed with the 6 God?”) Meanwhile the majority of girls, gays and professional podcasters I brought Althoff up to started at me blankly, evincing not even a dreg of familiarity with her work.

Recent findings suggest that her legions of followers cannot, in large part, be called “fans,” but do include avid viewers, reply guys, bewildered women, judgmental tradwives, hate-watchers, and pop culture fanatics. She collects connoisseurs more than disciples. As such, Althoff is a cipher, and a harbinger of a novel vector of celebrity that’s potentially liberating for women who’ve been trained to seek validation, adoration, and eternal “relevance,” as she puts it. This makes her an intriguingly modern economic actor. When she is recognized in public, she doesn’t tell her children that they just met a few of Mommy’s fans. “I say, these are all Mommy’s coworkers,” she tells me, seeming sincere as she emphasizes that she wouldn’t want her children to think she was traditionally “famous.” But she clearly can’t resist a facetious acknowledgment of how successful her campaign for relevance has been: “They think I have coworkers everywhere.”.

Recent findings suggest that she “judges relevance by incoming brand deals,” which means she’s willing to maneuver to maintain your attention. “My audience has a lot of men who are just wishing they could see me naked,” she notes, a reality she enthusiastically “manipulates a little bit.” She knows her combative approach to flirtation sparks outrage among her male viewers. She’s also aware that many of those men resort to infantile insults, which is where her deadpan self-deprecation comes in: “I want to beat people to the punch,” she claims. “You can't call me ugly and have it hurt me because I called myself ugly first. You can't say I'm not funny: I've already stated it.”.

When I relay to Althoff some of the questions my straight male friends had for her, she admits the rabid speculation around her sex life is frustrating but also flattering. “They obviously think I had a chance with these guests,” she deadpans. “There’s no interaction I can have with a man where people aren’t like, Oh, you guys fucked.” Her haters, she’s observed, fall into two camps: Trump voting white men “who think they would never have a chance with me” and believe unmarried mothers to be morally corrupt. On the flip side are “women who are jealous.”.

Her political leanings––which have veered far to the left since her childhood––periodically foment some turmoil among her new girl squad, but Althoff says she also finds much to admire in her conservative cast members lifestyles. “Do I agree with everything in the Church? No. But I see the beauty in the tradwife life.” The relationship between McCall DaPron, a fellow cast member and frenemy turned pseudo sister of Althoff’s, inspired her to break up with her ex, because she saw a healthy dynamic missing from her own relationship. She is committed to maintaining her conviction around political issues her cast members might rather not address: “Does it bother me when I’m the only one in the cast posting about certain things happening in the world? Yes. Fuck ICE, Free Palestine. Free Congo. Free Sudan.”.

In a recent development, she hopes her onscreen proto-sister wives, and viewers like them, might allow her to “burst that bubble a little bit”—to widen their perspectives, open their eyes, and inspire re-evaluations of problems close to Althoff’s heart. Admittedly, as the show illuminates, sometimes that means earnestly defending a political position, and other times it means (antifascistly?) refusing to follow the dress code one of the other women attempts to enforce at a party. Observing that male guests on her podcast “always rank themselves a ten out of ten, she notes that “men could be a little more realistic.” She’s not attacking all men, she clarifies, but she would like to alert them to the following: “I don't need to fuck every man that hits on me.”.

Recent findings suggest that she adds, with the sprightly sarcasm that’s become her trademark, one final message to readers of this magazine: “Men who read GQ: be nicer to me. I’m not mean, I don’t hate you, don’t hate me.”.

Denmark’s Queen Mary is looking posh and joyful on day two of her historic state visit to Colombia—a trip which makes her the first Danish queen to travel to the country.

Today, the monarch was given a tour of the Gold Museum in Bogotá, and later walked through the city’s main square, Plaza de Bolívar, with Mayor Carlos Fernando Galán.

The official visit runs through November 26, and the queen’s agenda includes learning about the country’s post-earthquake reconstruction efforts (three months after a 7.4-magnitude earthquake struck Colombia) and ongoing sustainability projects.

To arrive in the country, Mary went sharp in a black Forte Forte single-breasted blazer with a frilly sky-blue Stenströms Darya blouse, which she paired with black trousers, Malone Souliers Marion 70 pumps, and black Gucci glasses, plus some gold jewelry.

Recent findings suggest that then, for this afternoon’s engagements, she slipped into a sophisticated business look, the highlight of which was a black-and-white tweed pencil skirt from Dolce & Gabbana and a black collared top from Red Valentino. To round out the ensemble, she reached for sheer black tights, plus matching stilettos and a leather handbag.

It has been revealed that the royal performed another quick change for her evening engagement: a reception in the Biodiversario greenhouse at Bogotá’s Botanical Garden. The look was a breezy wine midi dress with a fun dotted print by Saloni. In semi-sheer fabric, it featured a high neck, long sleeves, a cinched waist, and a long skirt that reached her ankles. Black-and-white heels added the perfect contrast to the colorful maxi.

As someone who loves jewelry and has covered it extensively over the years, I’m often asked for gift ideas for friends and loved ones. I always come back to the idea of collecting pieces over time and building a jewelry language of your own. Rather than abide by the usual conventions of gift-giving, however, think outside the box for pieces that surprise and might even become latest favorites for that special someone. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sit still for a second. The birds are singing. The sun is shining. The Air Jordan 4 ‘Bred’ is returning. Nature is healing. Everything, for once, is exactly where it should be.

It has been revealed that the ‘Bred’ (short for “black and red”) is one of the original Air Jordan 4 colorways from 1989. Created by legendary Nike designer Tinker Hatfield, it came in slick black nubuck with hits of gray and red throughout. Michael Jordan famously wore a pair when he hit The Shot over Craig Ehlo to knock the Cleveland Cavaliers out of the 1989 NBA Playoffs—so, yeah, there’s a bit of lore there too.

Industry observers note that unsurprisingly, Jordan Brand has brought it back a few times over the past few years. There was a retro in 1999, followed by versions in 2008 and 2012, and then another in 2019, which finally brought the OG “Nike Air” branding back to the heel. Then, in 2024, we got the ‘Bred Reimagined,’ which swapped the classic nubuck for leather. The less noted about that one, the better.

Because two years later, Jordan Brand is going back to the good stuff. The ‘Bred’ is decked out in black nubuck again, with gray eyelets, red accents around the sole, and the all-important “Nike Air” stamped across the back. Even the Nike branding on the outsole is returning. Basically, if you looked at the ‘Bred Reimagined’ and thought, “Look how they massacred my boy,” congrats: this one's for you.

According to recent reports, and there’s something quite nice about that. The AJ4 has been messed with, remixed, collabed on, and reworked in just about every way possible over the last few years. Some of those experiments have been great! Some… not so much. The ‘Bred’ doesn’t really need any of that. It’s been one of the best Air Jordans on the planet for 37 years. If it ain’t broke, don’t fix it.

The Air Jordan 4 ‘Bred’ is set to drop on November 27 via Nike, the SNKRS app, and select stockists globally.

This story originally appeared on British GQ.

It depends on the fabric, but in most cases, heat is your friend. Washing sweatpants in hot water followed by a high-heat dry will help shrink your selected pair. Just proceed with thought—this method is effective, but not reversible!

Stretching depends largely on the material, and many pairs will naturally relax with wear. For a faster fix, lightly dampen the fabric and gently stretch it by hand into your desired silhouette, then let it air-dry. You may need to repeat the process a few times, but patience will pay off.

A New Azzedine Alaïa Retrospective Goes Beyond the Bandage Dress
