⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the bandage dress.
  • Alaïa’s designs “were completely shocking” to the public at the time, recounts Laura Camerlengo, curator in charge of costume and textile arts at the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco.
  • Born in 1935 in Tunis, Alaïa first trained as a sculptor, a background evident in his body of work.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the bandage dress. The zipper dress. The perforated leather. The jersey hoods. The peplummed chemises. Azzedine Alaïa’s designs may not look so radical now, but almost 50 years ago, he changed the collective tide of fashion. The bandage dress is perhaps the most pervasive bit of his legacy, and it is emblematic of how the late French-Tunisian designer ushered in a latest body-conscious silhouette in the ’80s, one made possible by technological innovations in materials that sculpted without any rigid, waist-cinching structure.

Alaïa’s designs “were completely shocking” to the public at the time, recounts Laura Camerlengo, curator in charge of costume and textile arts at the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco. She has spent the past four years developing a fresh exhibition titled “Azzedine Alaïa: Sculpting Fashion,” the first major U.S. retrospective dedicated to the work of the famed couturier. It opened November 21.

Born in 1935 in Tunis, Alaïa first trained as a sculptor, a background evident in his body of work. In 1956, he decamped to Paris to pursue fashion full-time. After a brief internship at the house of Christian Dior, he worked under Guy Laroche for less than two years before taking on his own private clients, then launching his own atelier in the late ’70s. From there, he built the house we know today. His obsession with construction and material innovation allowed him to both celebrate and liberate the female form. He passed away in late 2017 at the age of 82.

In a recent development, camerlengo first encountered Alaïa’s work as an assistant on the “Patrick Kelly Runway of Love” exhibition that the Philadelphia Museum of Art organized in 2014. “I was intrigued by how many of the newly introduced designers in Paris at this time were being supported by US consumers and retailers,” she claims. After ascending to her new position in San Francisco years later, she cold-emailed Olivier Saillard, director of the Azzedine Alaïa Foundation in Paris. He was intrigued, and the two began working together on the exhibition almost immediately.

Sources indicate that the exhibition focuses on 80 garments from across Alaïa’s celebrated career, divided over a series of archetypes—the bandage dresses, sculptures and shapes, black and white, silhouettes and suiting, and construction and craftsmanship—to explore how his design aesthetic evolved. Interspersed are designs worn by devotees like Tina Turner, Grace Jones, and Rihanna. One final gallery highlights his personal collections of the work of designers he most admired, like Christian Dior and Charles James.

Ahead, Camerlengo speaks to Bazaar about curating the fresh exhibition, contextualizing Alaïa’s work in today’s fashion landscape, and his enduring legacy.

The exhibition is not chronological. We look at a series of Alaïa’s archetypes like the bandage dress to explore how his design aesthetic evolved over the course of his career. He often himself said that he didn’t want to conform to seasonal trends; he was more interested in the evolution of his designs. And so the gallery shows a mix of objects dating from the 1980s to his final collection in 2017, and they’re largely grouped by type.

Sources indicate that when you come in, you are greeted by Grace Jones, as we say, and the seminal purple hooded bandage dress from the fashion Oscars [a French event held in 1985]. As you move through, you’ll see a selection of the zipper dresses, the chiffon gowns, and other works that tie into some of the other themes. In each space, we mix the time periods. And that was something Alaïa himself often said. [He had a running joke that he didn’t know his own age.] He often said he was “as old as the pharaohs.” Basically, time was a construct for him.

That’s a great word for it. We could think of the popularity of the Japanese fashion designers who obscured women’s bodies with their voluminous styles. We could think of the suiting of the period. The 1970s is this period of workplace equality. Women are wearing suits in the style of masculine dress, but that also means they're obscuring their bodies. And then we can think of pop culture. I always think of Diane Keaton’s Annie Hall in 1977.

Some of the individuals I interviewed for my catalog text who were retailers in San Francisco at the time described Alaïa's designs as being like a whiplash. It was a complete 180 from the styles that they had gotten used to over the past decade, which also includes the rise of T-shirts and jeans for women as a mode of dress.

So here you have these very sexy, very form-fitting clothes. And part of the Alaïa aesthetic, as I see it, is the reclamation of the gaze. Rather than women being passively looked at—usually by men—they are instead commanding their own agency. As you remarked, it was completely earth-shattering and very shocking at the time.

Industry observers note that azzedine Alaïa was one of the few couturiers who could work completely by the methods of tailoring and by draping, start to finish, from the initial concept to the final product. I did not fully appreciate his tailoring and the suits he constructed beforehand. We have a selection of them in a gallery of the exhibition, and their construction is absolutely incredible. The way they fit the body, the way they uplift and empower women through cloth—again, very antithetical to what we saw in the decades prior in the 1970s. These are very form-fitting, tailored at the waist, but they have soft feminine touches as well that give you this interesting mix of femininity and strength at the same time.

According to recent reports, very important. We talk in the first gallery about how women, speaking generally, were the architects of his life. He learned to sew from his sister, who was working for a seamstress. He was encouraged by a local midwife in Tunisia to go to school at the Institute of Fine Arts. She helped him forge his papers to read 16—he was only 15 at the time. He learned his skills, not in formal training, but from women in Tunisia.

In a recent development, and then his early work was supported by a lot of leading figures of international society, including various Rothschilds, the French performer Arletty, the Swedish American actress Greta Garbo, and that's all before he even started to work formally under his own label in the 1980s. Of course, in the 1980s, he adopts Naomi Campbell, who becomes his protégé. He has close relationships with Grace Jones and Tina Turner. They were hugely vital to him. In the exhibition, the clear invisible mounts that we use are actually based on the body of Naomi Campbell.

Sources indicate that probably the Grace Jones bandage dress from the fashion Oscars in 1985. Not only is it the progression of the bandage dress style that he experiments with throughout the course of the 1980s, but it represents a key moment in his career where he receives two very high accolades as part of the fashion Oscars and he’s recognized for his genius.

As far as the designs themselves, I think we would consider the bandage dress, for example, an iconic symbol of late 20th- and 21st-century fashion developed by Azzedine Alaïa, but of course iterated upon extensively. We've seen surges and resurgences in its popularity ever since.

And then as far as the landscape of the broader fashion system, Alaïa was someone who really eschewed seasonal calendars and trends. He was unconcerned with making things for the market. He often wanted to just produce clothes and share them when he felt they were ready. So I think his method of working foreshadows some of the conversations we’re having now about the overproduction of fashion and the overconsumption of fashion, even the detrimental environmental impacts that we see connected to it. He was really a forerunner, in a sense, to question the fashion system.

You can see how he really studied the construction of other garments and then adapted it in his own way in his designs. For example, he admired the work of Charles James, the great American fashion designer who was able to manipulate fabric to achieve weightless volume. And you see in Alaïa's own collections as he continues in his career, he does radial tucks and pleating to also get a certain amount of weightless volume in some of his gowns, very much in the spirit of James.

I hope our visitors appreciate the artistry of his work, first and foremost, and also the importance of handcraftsmanship. We are increasingly in an age of technology, especially with the rise of AI. What he created by his own hand is something that we can really marvel at.

It has been revealed that but sometimes you're strapped for time and have too much on your plate (pun intended) to whip something up from scratch. So we tried six different grocery store pumpkin pies to find the best store-bought shortcut. And our team's verdict was pretty unanimous, even if it’s a bit hard to hear: No premade pie will ever taste as good as a homemade one.

It primarily comes down to the crust. Frozen and pre-baked pies typically rely on vegetable-based fat instead of butter because they’re more affordable, reliable, and shelf-stable—but that comes at a cost. You not only miss out on the decadent, buttery taste, but the crusts can also leave an unpleasant film on your tongue.

That mentioned, when you need to outsource to the grocery store, we found two options that will work in a pinch.

Sources indicate that the pie that we’d feel most confident bringing to Thanksgiving dinner comes straight from the Whole Foods bakery department. That’s not to say it’s perfect, though. The crust is almost upsettingly pale, but it’s made with real butter and only a little bit of palm oil. And since it doesn’t leave a noticeable film and still lets the butter flavor shine, we’ll let this one slide.

According to recent reports, once you look past the crust’s color, this pie is solid overall. The filling is decadent, not too sweet, and creamy without being mushy. Whole Foods doesn’t shy away from the spices, either.

Senior Editor Samantha MacAvoy noted that the warming spices are nicely balanced, while Designer Alison Dominguez said, “The flavor was exactly how a pumpkin pie should taste.”.

Industry observers note that costco’s pumpkin pie isn’t perfect: The crust uses palm oil-based shortening rather than butter and can develop a soggy bottom if you buy it too far in advance. (And it doesn’t hold a candle to the warehouse’s holy grail pumpkin cheesecake.) But it has a cult following for a reason, and not just because of its $5.99 price tag.

Recent findings suggest that even with its faults, the crust has great flavor and enough salt to create a balanced bite. Dominguez appreciated how it was “flaky and not too thick, and most importantly, it let the pie filling itself shine.” News and Features Editor Amanda Mactas chose Costco’s pie as her number one pick. “It all seemed to melt together in one creamy bite,” she said.

And at over three pounds, this dessert is the indisputable champion if you want to feed a crowd for less.

Why Weed Might Actually Be Bad for Your Sleep

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (704 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gq

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Weed is, at this point, a widely used sleep aid.
  • The study, which was performed by Northwestern University researchers and published in JAMA Network, looked at 1,266 adults who participated in the Coronary Artery Risk Development in Young Adults (CARDIA) study, which followed participants for 35 years to determine how behavioral, biological, and environmental factors affected their risk of heart disease later in life.
  • Here’s what all of that means: Sleep efficiency is essentially how much of the time you spend in bed you’re actually asleep.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Everyone’s done it before. A pre-game gummy. A nighttime toke. Weed is, at this point, a widely used sleep aid. It usually works pretty well, too. But if you’ve made it a habit, you might just be sabotaging your shut-eye in the long run. According to a new October 2026 study, consuming pot in any form before bed causes people to have poorer quality of sleep—without them even realizing it. In other words: It has exactly the opposite of its intended effect. Here’s what you should know before popping an edible before you doze off.

The study, which was performed by Northwestern University researchers and published in JAMA Network, looked at 1,266 adults who participated in the Coronary Artery Risk Development in Young Adults (CARDIA) study, which followed participants for 35 years to determine how behavioral, biological, and environmental factors affected their risk of heart disease later in life. Of that sample size, 891 wore wrist-based activity monitors for at least a week so that researchers could examine their sleep patterns. After analyzing the data, the researchers found that those who were long-term cannabis owners had “poorer objective sleep, including lower sleep efficiency, greater fragmentation, and more time awake during the night,” Dr. Thanh-Huyen Vu, an author of the study and a research associate professor of preventive medicine at Northwestern University’s Feinberg School of Medicine, tells GQ.

Here’s what all of that means: Sleep efficiency is essentially how much of the time you spend in bed you’re actually asleep. So, lower sleep efficiency means spending more time lying awake instead of sleeping while sleep fragmentation refers to how often your sleep is interrupted, like when you’re unknowingly tossing and turning to get comfortable. The researchers also looked at how much total time participants spent awake during the night. It all boils down to the fact that long-term cannabis people weren’t sleeping as soundly or as continuously throughout the night—sometimes without them even knowing it.

The researchers can’t say for certain. Because the study was observational, it only established an association between long-term cannabis exposure and poorer sleep quality.

One possibility, Vu suggests, is that cannabis may “alter normal sleep architecture,” potentially changing the way the body cycles through different sleep stages.

Over time, it’s those changes that can contribute to more nighttime awakenings, which result in less restorative sleep. She notes more research is needed to understand the underlying biological mechanisms.

Recent findings suggest that deep sleep is one of the most important stages of sleep because it’s the phase when your body recovers physically, processes memory, and regulates the immune system. Interruptions in sleep result in less time during the deep sleep cycle, which inhibits your body from doing all the important things that help you function properly when you’re awake. The less deep sleep you get, the worse you feel in the morning. The reason why participants don’t pick up on these mid-sleep wake-ups is that they’re easy to forget. “Sleep trackers can capture some of these patterns, even when people don’t perceive their sleep as being particularly poor,” Vu says. It’s the same way in which you think you slept eight hours one night but woke up feeling groggy regardless.

Not necessarily. Given the sample population—middle-aged adults—the results may not apply to people in other age ranges or even those who use cannabis for medical reasons. Still, Vu says it’s important for people to understand that cannabis’s relationship with sleep may be more complicated than simply helping you drift off faster.

According to recent reports, if you regularly use cannabis before bed, paying attention to your sleep patterns may help you better understand how it’s affecting you. Wearable sleep trackers can offer some insight into nighttime awakenings and sleep efficiency, but you won’t get the same sleep analysis if you were part of a study like this. It might be worth trying out a period where you don’t use weed to fall asleep to see if it makes a difference in whether you feel more well-rested, or your mind feels sharper. Though the study still leaves a lot of questions to be answered, its data is clear enough to make anyone with a nightly gummy habit reconsider.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

It’s been living rent-free in my mind for the better part of this year: Conner Ives’s silk brocade opera coat, which captured nearly every fashion lover’s heart when it debuted on the fall/winter 2026 runway at London Fashion Week. Reminiscent of Mary-Kate Olsen’s fur-trimmed Balmain coat from the 2013 Met Gala, this particular stunner, along with the designer’s other iterations, seems to be what every It girl is wearing.

The coat—crafted with silk tapestries dating back to the Qing dynasty and with hand-embroidered depictions of red-crowned cranes, bamboo leaves, and flowers—was undoubtedly the first wave in what would become a tsunami of a trend: opera coats. And while plenty of faux fur-trimmed coats have made their way onto the market, those featuring Chinese imagery like that on Ives’s iterations have taken center stage.

“There’s been a real change in how people perceive Chinese design,” Cheryl Leung, founder and creative director of Sau Lee, tells ELLE. Leung attributes the opera coat’s rise in popularity to fashion’s shift away from minimalism and consumers’ growing appetite for expressive pieces, richer fabrics, and textures. “Brocade is a great example because it has so much character,” she claims. “The fabrics can be quite ornate, but when you put them into a modern silhouette or style them with something very simple, they feel completely different.”.

Recent findings suggest that chinese design has often been presented through a Western lens, but designers like Leung and Kim Shui are creating work rooted in their own cultural perspectives. Shui, the Chinese-American, New York-based creative director behind her eponymous label, has long been drawn to Chinese garments and the ways they communicate identity. “I’m particularly interested in the visual language and craftsmanship of traditional Chinese garments, whether it’s the silhouette of the qipao (a traditional Chinese dress dating back to the Qing dynasty), the richness of brocade, or traditional techniques like embroidery and intricate knot closures,” Shui tells ELLE. “I look at these elements not as things to reproduce literally, but as a vocabulary that I can reinterpret.”.

While the trend has gained widespread popularity, the Chinese design details behind it can sometimes be overlooked. “I’ve seen so many ‘trending winter coat’ videos featuring Chinese brocade coats with fur trim and traditional Chinese embroidered silk coats, but they don’t make any reference to their Chinese origins,” Shui says. “Instead of using terms like ‘qipao’ or ‘mandarin collar,’ creators will often describe these details generically as a ‘stand collar’ or ‘high neckline.’ It’s important to acknowledge where these design elements come from and the history behind them—why erase the cultural context?”.

Recent findings suggest that leung sees the coat’s popularity as an opportunity to bring attention to its history and the designers reinterpreting it. Shui and her team have also been creating content about the histories of brocade, embroidery, and the qipao, as well as the cultural references behind her collections to bring more awareness of the craft to her audience.

It has been revealed that “I do think there’s a difference between appreciating a design tradition and overlooking where it came from,” Leung claims. “If a designer has been inspired by Chinese textiles, craftsmanship, or traditional clothing, acknowledging that doesn’t take anything away from their creativity. If anything, it gives the work more depth and helps people appreciate the original references.” Shui adds that brands outside the culture have a “responsibility to acknowledge their origins rather than presenting them as an entirely new aesthetic.”.

In a recent development, fashion has been both a vehicle for cultural exchange and a product of it—and trends will undoubtedly come and go. Not everyone will be interested in the cultural history of the piece they buy—and Leung doesn’t necessarily think they need to be. Shui is happy to see people from all backgrounds embrace garments from outside of their own cultures. “I hope this renewed interest encourages people to look beyond the garment itself and discover the rich traditions and craftsmanship behind it,” she says.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, while male breast cancer is rare, estimates suggest that more than 2,600 men are diagnosed with an invasive form of the disease each year in the United States, and more than 500 die, according to the American Cancer Society.
  • There isn’t a universal description of what breast cancer lumps look like in men, but there are some common characteristics to keep in mind.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, if you’re like most guys, you probably have plenty of little bumps and lumps on your skin. There’s the callus on your toe from training for that 10K, the razor bumps along your neck from this morning’s shave, and the skin tag on your underarm you keep meaning to get removed. While it’s often completely fine to ignore these bumps, that isn’t always the case. Some can be a red flag worth paying attention to—especially if they’re on your chest.

According to recent reports, while male breast cancer is rare, estimates suggest that more than 2,600 men are diagnosed with an invasive form of the disease each year in the United States, and more than 500 die, according to the American Cancer Society. And one of its telltale signs is a firm bump under or near your nipple. Below, find out more about what a breast-cancer lump may look like and four other things that could be to blame for a new bump on your chest.

There isn’t a universal description of what breast cancer lumps look like in men, but there are some common characteristics to keep in mind. “Breast cancer in men typically presents as a painless, firm, or hard lump,” indicates Jose Pablo Leone, MD, the director of the Program for Breast Cancer in Men at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute in Boston.

Recent findings suggest that another sign that the bump could be breast cancer is if it’s behind or very close to the nipple and areola. “Men have much less developed breast glandular tissue than women, which is why breast cancer in men most commonly develops near or behind the nipple,” notes Dr. Leone. As for size even a lump as small as a pea can be cancerous, but by the time men go to the doctor, tumors are often larger than a marble, according to Dr. Leone. “In part because of the lack of awareness and screening, most men present with larger tumors,” he says. “But any size is worth mentioning to your doctor. Not all breast cancers feel the same, so any upcoming or persistent breast lump should be evaluated by a healthcare professional.”.

Industry observers note that your chest has a lot of oil glands, which can set the stage for pimples. “Staying in a sweaty shirt after a workout can make chest acne flare, especially if the fabric is tight and rubs against your skin,” indicates Elizabeth Bahar Houshmand, MD, a board-certified dermatologist based in Dallas. While blackheads and whiteheads are typically small and easy to identify, inflamed pimples or nodules may seem more alarming because they can be hard, painful, and form deep under the skin. When it comes to nodular acne specifically, you can’t treat it on your own. If that’s what you think you’re dealing with, see a dermatologist, who can prescribe an oral or topical medication to help clear it up.

“This is a collection of fat that forms under the skin,” says Sonya Kenkare, MD, a board-certified dermatologist at Illinois Dermatology Institute in Hinsdale, Illinois. “It is usually soft, not painful, and you can move it around in all different directions.” You don’t need to do anything about a lipoma, but if you want to get it removed, you can talk to a doctor about it.

According to recent reports, when hair follicles get inflamed or infected, you can end up with folliculitis. “Folliculitis often looks like small pimples or pus-filled bumps centered around a hair follicle” says Dr. Houshmand. “They may itch or feel tender.”.

Sources indicate that blockage or damage to a hair follicle can also cause epidermal inclusion cysts. These cysts occur when dead skin cells get trapped under the surface instead of shedding. “They feel somewhat firm and often have a central little black spot,” says Dr. Kenkare. Sometimes simply applying a warm compress to the area can help a cyst heal on its own, but a doctor can also inject it with a steroid to reduce swelling, drain it, or surgically remove it.

Recent findings suggest that this condition occurs when breast tissue gets enlarged in men, and it can first appear as a lump under your nipple. “It often feels like a rubbery or firm disc beneath the nipple, and it may be tender,” says Dr. Houshmand. While gynecomastia can come on as a side effect of some medications, like antibiotics or antidepressants, or diseases like thyroid disorders, sometimes there is no clear cause at all.

If you’re starting to feel like it’s difficult to tell on your own what the lump on your chest might be, you’re not wrong. That’s why it’s best to have your primary care physician look at any upcoming, unexplained bumps and tell you whether you need imaging, like a mammogram with an ultrasound. That may sound scary, but it’s really just covering your bases. “Uncommon things are uncommon, and breast cancer in men is uncommon,” says Dr. Leone. “You shouldn’t worry excessively about male breast cancer, but you should be aware of it.”.

Sources indicate that we may earn commission from links on this page, but we only recommend products we love. Promise.

A “baecation” often entails a romantic getaway, passionate activities, and a lot of vacation sex. But what if traveling with your significant other meant a lot of difficult conversations, a heated back-and-forth, and working to fix your relationship. I know: this sounds nothing like the dreamy R&R you pictured—but for some couples, it’s exactly what they planned for.

According to Booking.com’s 2027 Travel Predictions, 58 percent of U.S. travelers noted they would consider taking a trip to resolve conflicts or arguments.

Now, traveling itself already can cause real strain and arguments on relationships on its own. In the same data set, more than one-third of respondents noted they found out they were incompatible with their companion after a trip. Nearly three in 10 people have considered ending a relationship or friendship over a trip, while more than one in five have actually cut a vacation short because of a bad travel companion.

In a recent development, but if you’re already having relationship issues with your partner, is a trip a good idea? People still seem to think so. About 81 percent said that taking part in at least one vacation activity with another person helps them have honest or difficult conversations.

So should you be planning a trip the next time you and your partner start arguing?

A change of scenery might be exactly what you and your partner need to see eye-to-eye again.

“Getting away from work, chores, kids, in-laws, or house and childcare stuff can lower defenses,” couples therapist Justena Kavanagh tells Cosmopolitan.

She explains that when you’re home, you’re essentially having every argument on the same “battleground.”.

Industry observers note that “Somewhere upcoming often brings back the honeymoon period, when you could really see each other without life’s stresses in the way,” she claims. And if both you and your partner have busy lives and packed schedules, a vacation may really be the only time you can focus on the challenges in your relationship without distraction.

In a recent development, plus, vacations encourage you to relax—which can go a long when in an argument. “When we’re rested, we’re more regulated, and when we’re regulated, we can listen instead of defending,” Kavanagh notes.

She explains that it’s important to establish why exactly you’re going on the vacation in the first place. Are you getting away to talk about an problem? Or simple to get away from it and reconnect? Agreeing on the purpose for the trip before you start packing your bikini will help you and your partner get on the same page—so you don’t end up just arguing more later.

“Trips suit conversations about connection, like feeling distant, intimacy, or where the relationship is going,” she says. Other things like finances or in-law conflicts may need a follow-up at home.

If you decide that you’re going to talk your issues out, remember that you are still on vacation. That doesn’t mean everything has to be wonderful, of course. But Kavanagh encourages couples to treat the trip like a summit. This means talking early in the day (after a good night’s rest) and working on things while taking breaks.

The trip should essentially be your opportunity to discuss what’s right now happening in the relationship, where you want the relationship to go, and how to shift priorities to get there.

Sure, a beautiful view and hotel sex will definitely lighten the mood and probably even make you more agreeable—but it isn’t a magical bandaid for your relationship problems.

“If couples don’t have relational skills at home, they won’t miraculously have them on vacation,” Kavanagh warns.

It has been revealed that so if you’re going to go on a vacation to work on things with your partner, you’re going to want to put a plan into place. The best method? Talking about the pattern behind the argument, rather than hyperfocusing on the latest incident.

And even if you do come to a resolution on vacation, make sure you’re setting a plan in place for the positive energy to flow into your everyday lives.

Sources indicate that “Be realistic about home, where you’re more stressed and old patterns return fast,” Kavanagh says. “Proposal follow-up support, a regular check-in, and what you’ll do when things go off track, because they will.”.

Sources indicate that okay, so not all of us can afford to book a flight every time we get into an argument with our partner—but you don’t have to. Out of all the activities that people do on vacation, respondents said that it was mostly hikes or walking that was the most effective at getting them to open up and have the difficult conversations.

Lucky for you, taking a hike is totally free—and can do wonders for whatever issue you may be facing with your partner.

Kavanagh explains that walking and hiking take pressure off of an argument.

Recent findings suggest that “Face to face can feel like a confrontation; side by side, you’re facing the same direction and don’t have to hold eye contact in the hardest moments,” she explains. This is something we see in psychotherapy: think about someone lying on a couch, looking at the ceiling. This helps physiologically and emotionally. Plus the actual physical activity helps, too.

“Walking also discharges stress and is a natural form of bilateral stimulation, the left-right rhythm used in therapies like EMDR,” she indicates.

It has been revealed that when your partner is irritating you, it’s likely that the last thing you want to do is travel with them. But if you’re determined to move past whatever may be causing a rift, that might be exactly what you need.

Honeymoons and other happy occasions shouldn’t be the only time we travel with our partners with the purpose of growing closer, reconnecting, and strengthening the relationship. Sometimes, even in hardship, a little getaway could be the jumpstart your relationship needs to get back on track. Just remember that after the vacation ends, you do have to go back to reality.

“The good feelings are real, but the test is whether they last back home, where life is harder,” Kavanagh says.

The Best Moisturizers for Softer, Smoother, More Resilient Skin After 40

📅 01 Feb 2024 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1526 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As I write this, it’s two days before Thanksgiving in Chicago, and I’m tending to my prep work; to clarify, I don’t mean peeling potatoes.
  • In a recent development, “In your 40s, you may notice changes in your skin, including increased dryness, fine lines, loss of elasticity, and a decrease in overall radiance,” said Patty Aguilar, one of the spa’s esthetician.
  • According to recent reports, A common mistake she sees older women making is focusing only on hydration while overlooking ingredients that can improve skin texture and tone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As I write this, it’s two days before Thanksgiving in Chicago, and I’m tending to my prep work; to clarify, I don’t mean peeling potatoes. At 46, my skin gets ultra-dry this time of year, and getting ready for the holidays also means sourcing the best moisturizers for aging skin, lest I show up to seasonal celebrations looking dry and sallow—basically, anything but celebratory. So along with making a shopping list for the many side dishes in my future, I booked a Hydrating Facial at St. Regis Chicago’s spa—and maximized my time there by asking the team to fill me in on everything I need to know to stay moisturized at home.

In a recent development, “In your 40s, you may notice changes in your skin, including increased dryness, fine lines, loss of elasticity, and a decrease in overall radiance,” said Patty Aguilar, one of the spa’s esthetician. “At this stage, it's crucial to move beyond simply moisturizing and begin incorporating targeted ingredients that address your skin's changing needs while supporting its moisture barrier.”.

According to recent reports, A common mistake she sees older women making is focusing only on hydration while overlooking ingredients that can improve skin texture and tone. “I recommend looking for moisturizers that combine nourishing ingredients with gentle exfoliating or skin-renewing ingredients, such as lactic acid or fruit enzymes, when appropriate for your skin type,” she notes.

According to recent reports, and though thick, cushiony creams can often feel the most luxurious on parched skin—particularly as winter approaches—Aguilar emphasizes that the right texture depends on individual skin types. A thicker moisturizer isn't necessarily more effective. What matters most is the formulation and whether the ingredients address your skin's specific needs. With that in mind, we've tapped skincare pros to share the best formulas for redness, dry skin, daytime, and more below. Winter is coming—stay moisturized out there!

“Our bodies produce less elastin and collagen as we get older,” Saedi acknowledges. “In fact, collagen production begins to slow as early as your mid-twenties. We start losing one percent of our collagen per year after that. By 40, collagen drops more dramatically.” As collagen and elastin decline, fine lines, wrinkles, and sagging becomes more noticeable in the skin. “Your face also loses volume as you age, and your skin will become thinner,” Saedi claims.

But that’s not all. “Declining estrogen levels during perimenopause and menopause can also wreak havoc on your skin, contributing to dryness, dullness, thinning, and wrinkling in the skin,” Saedi claims. “Lastly, sun damage accumulates over your lifetime and is one of the biggest causes of lines, wrinkles and unwanted pigmentation, also commonly referred to as sun spots.”.

What is an ideal skincare regimen for mature skin?

According to Magovern, a morning skin care regime doesn’t have to start with face wash. “Don’t cleanse if skin feels dry or overprocessed, particularly if you did a good cleanse before bed,” she instructs. However, for mature skin that is “doing well and feeling strong,” she signs off on a gentle exfoliating cleanser that contains AHAs or PHAs.

Next up, a hydrating toner is “a great way to cleanse the skin without overwashing it,” she notes, noting that “water can actually act as an irritant.” Follow the toning step with a serum that contains antioxidants, such as vitamin C, to protect and restore the skin. “You can also look for a serum with chemical exfoliators,” Magovern adds. “These can help remove some of those older surface skin cells and help the skin retain its ability to hold onto moisture and bring back the glow.” A rich moisturizer, followed by SPF, caps off the ideal morning regime.

In the evening, “gentle cleansers or oil cleansers are great choices for mature skin,” Magovern continues. “I prefer a gentle cleanser at night because subsequent steps tend to include more active products.” Exfoliation can also be part of a nighttime regime one to three times a week. “It may not be intuitive, but exfoliating the skin can actually help moisturize it because it removes the surface dead cells, which make it harder for the moisturizers to penetrate and work effectively,” notes Magovern. “Exfoliators also help stimulate collagen production.” For mature skin, she recommends a chemical exfoliator with gentle AHAs like glycolic and lactic acids, and PHAs, like gluconolactone, which have moisturizing and antioxidant properties.

As a second-to-last step before bed, apply a treatment serum infused with active ingredients like retinol or peptides, which encourage cell turnover and cellular repair. “Sleep is the time when the cellular machinery is actively restoring and repairing, and it’s the perfect time to give the skin what it needs to help accomplish its nighttime work,” Magovern notes.

In a recent development, lastly, apply a face moisturizer that helps the skin attract and retain moisture overnight. “Occluding the skin with a moisturizer also allows the active ingredients in the previous steps to penetrate deeper and perhaps work more effectively,” she claims. “The moisturizing step is vital for nourishing and hydrating the skin while you sleep.”.

What ingredients work best in a moisturizer for aging skin?

“Hyaluronic acid and other humectants, like glycerin, are notable to help attract and retain water in the skin,” says Ashley Magovern, MD, a board-certified dermatologist in Manhattan Beach, California, and medical advisor for Dermstore. “But, other ingredients are important for aging skin as well. Once you attract the water, it’s important to trap it and prevent water loss.” Occlusive agents like jojoba-seed oil or shea butter help lock moisture into the skin, while ceramides—lipids that help maintain and repair the skin barrier—“are critical in a moisturizer,” Magovern says.

Additionally, “moisturizers that include retinol—or using a retinoid or retinol serum in addition to your moisturizer—can help improve the appearance of elasticity, texture, pigmentation and wrinkles,” claims Nazanin Saedi, MD, FAAD, a board-certified dermatologist in Philadelphia. “Caffeine helps plump the skin which can temporarily improve the appearance of sags and wrinkles. Other ingredients to look for would be ones that help stimulate and support the production of collagen: Peptides, vitamin C, niacinamide (vitamin B3), and growth factors.”.

What kind of texture is ideal in a moisturizer for aging skin?

It has been revealed that “As a rule of thumb, thicker consistencies are better at locking in moisture by literally creating a barrier on the skin’s outermost layer to prevent water from evaporating from the surface of the skin,” claims Tony Nakhla, DO, medical director of OC Skin Institute in Orange County and founder of Eighth Day. “The more occlusive a product is, the more hydrating.”.

Recent findings suggest that however, hydration isn’t the only factor to consider. “The viscosity or thickness of a moisturizer is not as important to its efficacy as the active ingredient,” offers Stacey Tull, MD, MPH, board-certified dermatologic surgeon and owner of St. Charles County Dermatologic Surgery in Missouri. “Thicker moisturizers such as shea butter may not be as effective for some skin types as a thinner hyaluronic-acid-based product or an oil-based serum. Even at an older age, some people are still acne-prone and a heavy moisturizer would not be a good option for them. Likewise, someone with dry, fragile skin may benefit from a thicker, more emollient ointment or cream.”.

What is the importance of a moisturizer for aging skin?

It has been revealed that A moisturizer for mature skin is “absolutely vital,” says Rachel Nazarian, MD, FAAD, a board-certified dermatologist at Schweiger Dermatology in Upcoming York City. She explains that one one of the key clinical markers of aging skin is its inability to create and retain moisture naturally. “Loss of moisture can make skin look more flaccid, less youthful, and dull,” Nazarian says.

Furthermore, “dry skin leads to inflammation, even if you can’t see it,” notes Magovern. “Inflamed skin will not tolerate all the active skin care products that we all want to use, so it’s imperative to keep that barrier strong. Furthermore, inflamed skin will trigger your skin problems like eczema, seborrheic dermatitis, and rosacea, so it’s important to keep the skin moisturized. Hydrated skin also just looks smoother, younger and brighter.” In short, she says: “There are so many reasons to moisturize.”.

Ingredients to Look for in a Moisturizer for Aging Skin.

The best moisturizers for aging skin contain key ingredients that tackle everything from dryness to sagging and dark under-eye circles. Below, top dermatologists and a plastic and reconstructive surgeon break down the best ingredients to look for when scouting out a moisturizer that can almost appear to rewind time—or at the very least, diminish the appearance of wrinkles.

What to Consider in a Moisturizer for Aging Skin.

According to recent reports, the best moisturizers for aging skin have just the right balance of rich, hydrating texture, anti-aging ingredients, and benefits tailored to one’s individual skin type. How to choose the right moisturizer for you? “Depending on your skin type—whether you are dry, oily, normal or combination—you may opt for different ingredients and formulation types, such as gel, lotion, or cream,” says Libby.

On another ingredient note, Libby says that it’s wise for those with sensitive skin to avoid potential irritants such alcohol, fragrances, and essential oils.

Whether it was roasting a chicken, pouring an outrageously large Cosmopolitan, or just organizing her pantry, I’d happily watch Ina Garten do just about anything on television. But there’s apparently one TV gig that even the Barefoot Contessa can't stomach, and I’m a little devastated we’ll never get to see it.

During the November 18 episode of her Happy Hour with Ina Garten podcast, Garten got to talking with guest Rose Byrne about opportunities that felt too intimidating to pursue. Ina didn’t have to think very hard to come up with her own example.

Sources indicate that “Somebody asked me to do Dancing with the Stars,” she revealed. “I thought, ‘Nobody needs to see that. That’s not happening.’”.

With which I respectfully disagree. I think quite a few of us would happily clear our schedules to see Ina Garten attempt a salsa. Unfortunately, Garten wasn’t particularly eager to find out how she'd fare in the ballroom. “The closer I got to the day when I had to do it, the more I’d have nightmares,” she admitted.

Byrne was sympathetic, acknowledging that she’d be terrified of competing, too.

Recent findings suggest that still, this is a woman who’s made some pretty bold decisions throughout her career. Garten left her job working on nuclear energy policy in Washington, D.C., to buy a specialty food store in the Hamptons with virtually no experience running one. There were some early mishaps, including a batch of roast chickens nobody wanted until she changed how they were displayed, and those experiences eventually helped shape the approachable cooking philosophy behind her hugely successful cookbooks.

It has been revealed that and Garten has certainly gotten comfortable sharing the spotlight over the years. In Delish’s recent interview with Garten and Jennifer Garner, the longtime friends traded stories about their kitchen adventures, favorite recipes, and even late-night In-N-Out Burger runs. Give Ina some good food and someone she loves spending time with, and she's in her element.

Personally, though, I can't stop imagining Jeffrey in the audience holding up a giant “10” sign in support of his wife. We really missed out on something special.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that iam here to debunk a common dating myth: Despite what all the relationship gurus might suggest, dating doesn’t have to be confined to the summer. In fact, some of the best, most romantic dates can happen during the late fall and dead of winter. After all, every street and tree is covered in twinkling lights and the cold weather gives you an excuse (not that you need one) to cozy up next to your crush. Add the festivities of the holiday season on top of all of that and you literally have the makings of a dream date.

Sure, the urge to snuggle up with your coziest blanket and binge your favorite rom-coms is nagging you and your person—I get it. But this holiday season is the time to make your Hallmark movie dreams a reality! Whether you’re looking for an option for a third date with someone you just started seeing or trying to keep things fresh and fun in your long-term relationship, there’s something on this list for you.

Sources indicate that volunteering as a date night is a great way to see someone’s generous side. Find a local donation center, soup kitchen, or a cause that means a lot to you. You’ll be able to tell a lot about your date by their reaction to this idea and how they carry themselves throughout the volunteering.

Sources indicate that this one will really test your teamwork. You can either grab a premade kit or go old-school and use a pint-sized milk carton and graham crackers as your base. Some of the premade are pretty simple, while others can be a bit more intricate. Either way, both will force you and your date to work together and problem solve. This will be a good way for those red flags or green flags to show themselves.

Because it’s time you get in on the whole matching pajamas and Santa hats. If you don’t want to put out money for a photographer, set up your phone’s camera with a timer and tripod—the photos can look just as amazing!

Elevate your hot chocolate game with fun flavors, like salted caramel, dark chocolate, or peppermint. You can buy premade variety packs or really chef it up with making your own. Whatever you choose, just be sure not to skim on the toppings. Grab marshmallows of all sizes, candy canes, whipped cream (I personally love the boozy vodka-infused peppermint one from Whipshots), and whatever else sounds enticing. You will be chocolate wasted and it will be fantastic.

According to recent reports, karaoke isn’t about who sounds the best but who has the best energy. Belt out your favorite holiday jams, from the classics to new renditions of the season’s most popular songs. It’s truly a perfect way to bond and see if your date can match your vibe.

This option is such a fun way to spend time together. Whether this is an early date with someone you recently started seeing or an activity you and your longtime love do, it’s great for talking, asking questions, and having fun. If you’re a part of the first group, this can be an opportunity to make a candle for each other—then you could exchange them as a low-stakes holiday gift (because getting a present for your situationship is always tricky).

If you or your date are people who appreciate a good aesthetic, finding a local light show could be the perfect night out. The low lighting and colorful moments can help you draw closer to your person, whether it’s in the car riding through or walking. Light shows leave room for more intimate conversations to take place, too, if you want that.

Recent findings suggest that the best way to spread holiday cheer is by supporting local businesses. From small batch food to unique clothes and accessories, it’s where you and your partner can shop for each other or grab gifts for loved ones. Oftentimes, these events also have other activities available nearby, like ice skating or photo moments, making for the perfect two-in-one date.

According to recent reports, bring out the creative energy with a cutesy arts and crafts moment. Grab a few blank ornaments, brushes and bottles of paint, stickers, fabric, and whatever else strikes your fancy. Set it all up on a flat surface (like a dining table or floor), throw in a few Christmas songs and snacks, and you’ve got the makings of a simple and fun at-home holiday date night.

Industry observers note that speaking of not making date night complicated, a simple stroll through your neighborhood (or perhaps one that’s more festive than yours) can still be made special. Make some boozy hot chocolates or hotty toddies, strap in to all your cold-weather gear, and sidewalk hike through your community. Bonus points for lots of hand holding, hugging, kissing and gossiping about the neighbors inflatable holiday characters in their front yard.

“Do you want to build a snowman?” Anna from Frozen isn’t the only one who can enjoy the feeling of holiday magic. Similar to ornament decorating and gingerbread house making, building a snowman is the ultimate nostalgia cheat code. While he might not come to life like Olaf, dressing him up with the cutest scarf and hat will still be just as worthwhile.

Recent findings suggest that the intentionality behind handwritten notes will forever show true thoughtfulness. This idea allows the two of you to really get creative with one another and reflect on who in your lives you want to wish a happy holiday season. Whether you’re sending our joint cards or individual ones, let your heartfelt emotions shine through.

Sources indicate that can you technically do this any time of the year? Yes. But walk with me: What makes sporting events special for the holiday season is the amount of on-the-ground activations and curated experiences that teams provide fans. I’m talking seasonal menus galore, holiday-themed lounges, and activations where you can put your partner’s competitive skills to the test. It’s almost like a bunch of dates in one!

In a recent development, warm up from the brisk cool air outside by attending a wine tasting at your local winery or private holiday-themed events. Wines with notes of cocoa, hints of spice, and earthiness are especially great to lean into for rich flavor. They also pair well with heavier meals that people typically enjoy during the winter months.

Love the snow but hate the cold? Search for the nearest igloo dining restaurant near you for a winter lunch or dinner. Usually, the igloos are kind of snug (but not in an uncomfortable way), giving you at-home levels of cozy with a space heater or bonfire. They’re also super festive with the decor, so you and your date will feel all the holiday cheer.

#134931. Photographer Franco Rubartelli Shares the Stories Behind Some of Vogue’s Most Famous ‘60s Shoots

📅 28 Aug 2017 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2766 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Vogue ↗ Open Full Page

Photographer Franco Rubartelli Shares the Stories Behind Some of Vogue’s Most Famous ‘60s Shoots

📅 28 Aug 2017 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2766 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Franco Rubartelli and Veruschka on location in Brazil.
  • Sources indicate that editor’s Note: Veruschka, the most super of ’60s models, has died.
  • The 1960s were a heady time of change and youth and fantasy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Franco Rubartelli and Veruschka on location in Brazil.

Sources indicate that editor’s Note: Veruschka, the most super of ’60s models, has died. Her love affair with Franco Rubartelli played out in the pages of Vogue. In memoriam we are revisiting this interview with the photographer who wrote of Veruschka on Instagram: “She wasn’t just a great model. She was an elegant woman, sensitive, brave, with a beauty that did not stay in the camera, it would get into the soul of whoever watched her. She had a way of being in the world that you don't learn; you take in. People like Veruschka don’t go away at all. They stay in a picture, in a perfume, in a song, in a way of smiling.”.

The 1960s were a heady time of change and youth and fantasy. This was also the case in Vogue, then led by Diana Vreeland, who brought her own taste for historicism and exoticism to its pages. “For Vreeland, everything impossible was possible,” says Franco Rubartelli, who, between 1964 and 1970, created some of the most memorable photographs ever published in the magazine. Presented in multipage spreads and taken in far-flung locales, these now-iconic images are exemplars of an elevated and romanticized hippie ethos. On a personal level, they documented one of fashion’s great love affairs.

Industry observers note that rubartelli, born in Florence, is a self-taught photographer who had planned to follow his father into the Italian Navy. He was pursuing his back-up blueprint, diplomacy, when Cupid arranged a collision that eventually steered him toward fashion. Enrolled at Cambridge to study English, Rubartelli recounts, he went to a pub to meet a blind date—who stood him up. As he rose to leave, he collided with a waitress carrying a tray of beer, which doused him. The tray bearer in question was a Swiss beauty named Françoise Schluter, earning pocket money at the pub while studying languages at the university. It was amore, and soon Rubartelli and Schluter were a couple. They married and lived in Rome with their son, Luigi. Tall, lithe, and blonde, Schluter was discovered on the streets there and started modeling. Her career transformed Rubartelli, by his own admission, into the archetypal jealous husband.

With her “scrubbed good looks,” Françoise Rubartelli models “American Sports Clothes in Italy.”.

Industry observers note that one night, after having mysteriously found a camera in their apartment, Rubartelli asked Schluter to pose for him on a beach. With no stylist, hair, or makeup—nor much knowledge of how the camera worked—he took pictures of the wife he feared he was losing, pictures that were infused with longing, youth, and freedom—qualities rarely expressed in the formal fashion photographs of the time. Having asked Schluter what the most key magazine was, Rubartelli got together some money to develop the film and secretly sent the results to Vogue.

In a recent development, much to Rubartelli’s surprise, he received a positive reply from New York in the form of a telegram, signed Diana Vreeland, then Vogue’s editor in chief, that read: “Beautiful model, beautiful pictures, will get in touch with you.” Soon, the photographer and his model wife were working with Consuelo Crespi, the magazine’s editor in Rome; their first story appeared in the August 1964 issue. As Rubartelli and Schluter were racking up credits and becoming known as a couple, though, their love story was unraveling. “We spent too much time together as photographer and model, and not enough as man and woman,” Rubartelli explains via email. Their final rupture (circa 1965) left Rubartelli “without work, without my wife, without my model, without my son.”.

In a recent development, another no-show launched the second chapter of Rubartelli’s Vogue career. Having received a call about an advertising job, the young photographer went to meet the client at the Parco dei Principi Grand Hotel in Rome. He remembers that as he waited, and waited some more, “a tall, skinny woman in a black cloak and long knee-high boots walked past and caught my attention.” Rubartelli asked the concierge who she was and was told she was a German model, at which point he called his mother and asked her to pose as his secretary and invite this alluring Vera von Lehndorff-Steinort, aka Veruschka, to stop by his studio with her portfolio. “At this point,” Rubartelli explains, “my name was known through my work for Vogue. Veruschka stopped by in the early afternoon and we talked until the evening. I invited her to dinner at a restaurant. We spoke about Françoise, and she told me about her family. We shared our problems and stayed talking like two parrots until an innkeeper told us it was closing time. It was very late. We spent the rest of that night and every successive night together for nearly nine years. It was love at first sight.”.

Theirs was a creative relationship that flourished in print and in life and took the pair around the globe. Recently Rubartelli, now living in Venezuela, has started to use Instagram as a biographical platform. Having spent endless hours poring over ’60s Vogues and becoming especially curious about Rubartelli and his models, his Instagram diary left me spellbound and eager to know more. I reached out to the ebullient Rubartelli, who openly and graciously agreed to share some personal stories with me.

Industry observers note that “You know something?” Rubartelli recently wrote, “I think that I have never been a photographer. I was simply a man who loved the two most crucial women of his life through his camera. I remember how beautiful my pictures came out when I was in love with Françoise or Veruschka, and when our stories ended, when there was no more feeling between us, I could stay for hours and hours in front of them without doing one good picture.” Rubartelli does himself a disservice. The Vogue archive provides evidence that he very much has a feeling for the form.

Here, the stories behind some of his best-known Vogue assignments.

“[After meeting and falling in love], we decided to take some photos together. Veruschka was very tall—her size was not commercial for the fashionable photos at that time—so we got to thinking about doing something different, and we came up with the idea of body painting. No one had been doing this.”.

“We bought colorful makeup, feathers, and paillettes and decided, on our own dime, to go to the island of Eleuthera in the Bahamas. There we painted Veruschka’s naked body.”.

Sources indicate that “During the time we shared together, I noticed that Veruschka carried with her inferiority complexes from her childhood. It sometimes felt as if she were not happy in her body, that her personality wanted to evade its physical dimension to become other beings. She found in makeup the possibility of escaping and transforming into other things: a butterfly that could fly, a panther or a tiger to run in the jungle, a mermaid to sink into the sea.”.

“We often went to Veruschka’s mother’s house in Petersrkirchen, near Munich. She was a very open-minded lady and very proud of Vera. She lived in a big house with many rooms. When we visited, our rooms were under the roof on the second floor. They were very big and all built in wood.”.

“Veruschka’s mother lived a drama with all her daughters during the Second World War. Her husband, [Heinrich Graf von Lehndorff-Steinort], participated in the plot to kill Hitler in his bunker. It was not successful, and he was executed. [According to Der Spiegel, Vera’s mother, Gottliebe, was first put in prison and then placed in a working camp with her newborn child. Her older daughters were moved, with other children of the resistance, to a nursing home and renamed.] Reunited after the war, they moved from one place to another and were very poor. When I met Vera’s mother, she had a boyfriend living with her. He was a crazy musician playing very heavy and noisy music. Her mother loved him and his music. In winter, the place was very beautiful. It was near a forest, and the fog made a great atmosphere.” From left: Countesses Catharina and Vera (known as Veruschka) von Lehndorff, Frau Marie Eleonora von Haeften, and Baroness Gabriela von Plotho.

“The Queen Christina assignment came about while we were watching the movie [about her] starring the tremendous Greta Garbo. Before the film was over, Veruschka and I simultaneously had the idea to propose the look of the queen to Diana Vreeland. Enthusiastic, we asked for an appointment with her and got one for the following week. This meant that we had to work day and night without sleeping to have the project ready with sketches. If we weren’t on time, we’d have to wait a long time to see her. We were always a little nervous about what Mrs. Vreeland’s reaction would be. She was a very straight woman; if she liked an idea, she would accept it right away; if she didn’t like it, we understood immediately that the project did not work for Vogue. She was very fond of us, but didn’t care about our reaction if she did not like the idea.”.

Sources indicate that “Mrs. Vreeland’s mysterious office [was infused] with the smell of her candle. How she walked, how she moved her hands with her long, expressive fingers, was very exotic. She created a magical atmosphere in her office, which had black walls full of photographs and furniture upholstered in an intense red fabric, mixed with leopard skins. In this dim environment you almost didn’t see Vreeland, who dressed all in black and red and almost matched the decor. ‘How are you, Mrs. Vreeland?’ asked Veruschka. We explained all the details and she listened in silence. It was a silence that was scary. Finally, when we finished, she got to her feet and congratulated us, saying: ‘This is so fabulous; let’s do it!’”.

It has been revealed that “Mrs. Vreeland loved the Queen Christina idea and ordered dresses to be made for Veruschka. We headed to Austria, where we made Innsbruck our base. For 10 days we looked for locations. It wasn’t easy to find a castle.”.

“Mrs. Vreeland almost never rejected an idea: Queen Christina, Libya, Texas, Australia, Brazil . . . . For Vreeland, everything impossible was possible, and she didn’t put limits on our creativity. This was very stimulating for us, because every project we proposed was more daring. I remember one time she called us by surprise and asked us to go to Rio de Janeiro to photograph some dresses during Carnival. She highlighted us the clothes and explained her idea to us. ‘Franco,’ she mentioned, ‘I do not want to see the Carnival; I want you to work in a studio with the windows opened. Franco,’ she continued, ‘I want, I want . . . pissst.’ She made a buzzing noise with her mouth closed. ‘I want you to shoot like that. Do you understand what I mean?’ I did not. It was impossible to understand what she meant with that sound.”.

“I think Mrs. Vreeland was very original. Having such an important position in the world of fashion in those years, she directed taste toward the different, the eccentric. She understood things immediately, and if she liked an idea, she approved it on the spot. She had very precise ideas about colors; for example, she loved red and dressed in it and decorated her apartment in it. Apart from her strong and precise ideas of color, one could never be sure about her decisions until the last moment. Once she liked an idea and authorized it, she approved the costs of the productions. There was never an intention to reduce the result by making any kind of economy.”.

Recent findings suggest that “I can assure you, without a doubt, that Veruschka, myself, and Giorgio di Sant’Angelo [a textile designer turned stylist and designer] were a creative team for a long period. We met together to develop themes, and if we had a trip that we liked, we gave ourselves to the story until we fully developed it. Veruschka and I really enjoyed going to Giorgio’s house. We spent many hours there thinking, drawing ideas, doing tests. Then, back in the city, we visited museums, bought books to study, saw films, all to perfect our ideas and to make sure of the look that we wanted to create.”.

“Giorgio [above right] was unlike anyone else; his creativity was superior. He had been born in Florence, Italy, but had spent so much time outside of the country that he had forgotten the language a little; when he spoke, it was a funny [argot]. He was an original and very imaginative designer. Giorgio was an excellent companion also in private life. He shared with his friends the joyful moments as well as the anxious ones and tried to creative a positive atmosphere. His style tended toward the exotic. His only defect was that he smoked too much; he was never without a cigarette in his hand. He was an artist in creating jewelry, and he himself was upholstered in necklaces of all kinds.”.

Sources indicate that “Giorgio loved colors and their mixture. I studied him as we prepared for our journey to the Painted Desert. In order to decide what fabrics to bring with us, he came to the studio with many samples of all colors. In front of a mirror he tested the various combinations by cutting and mixing the different pieces with incredible taste and perfection. It was fun to see him. He looked like a scarecrow all covered in pieces of cloth. For the final test shots on Veruschka, he invented the gypsy look by cutting all sorts of fabrics and wrapping them around the body.”.

“When we decided to work in the desert of Libya, we visited many stores looking for fabrics suitable for all the drapings that would be made on location. They weren’t sewn dresses, but draped on the body. We were creating a look, an atmosphere—nothing more. We went to Diana Vreeland to sell her an atmosphere, and she accepted it and gave us carte blanche. Of course, we had our sketches, but sometimes we were moved by feelings, or so inspired by the atmosphere, that we were forced to change things.”.

“Every morning in one location or another, Veruschka, almost naked, was standing for many hours as Giorgio draped on her body. These preparations were incredible. In the sand around us there were meters of fabric that Giorgio cut and adapted to her body. We had a long mirror that Veruschka could see herself in. Although we always started early in the morning, before dawn, these preparations lasted many hours, and I worried and complained because the light became too strong. We couldn’t work later than 10:00 a.m.; we could start again after 4:00 p.m. when the desert light turned gold.”.

Industry observers note that “I remember that when we traveled, Giorgio spent a lot of time researching, trying to find original clothes typical of each place we were visiting. Before our shoot in Ghadames, he went to visit the small souk of the town, where he discovered two small warehouses full of typical desert fabrics and bought many of them. As he did not have much money, he made a deal with the store owner, agreeing to swap the fabrics he had brought for the ones in the souk, so Giorgio returned to New York with stupendous finds.”.

Recent findings suggest that “Giorgio came to the desert shoot every day with two or three suitcases full of fabrics that he modeled on Veruschka’s body according to his state of mind. He spread the fabrics out on the ground so he could have a panoramic view of them all. One day a strong breeze blew in all of a sudden and the fabrics began to fly away. It was amusing to see Giorgio run after them in the dunes, and suddenly stumble and fall. Once we were approached by a little girl from Ghadames. She was very cute and watched us curiously. After a while she grabbed a piece of fabric and put it on her head, simulating what Giorgio was doing with Veruschka. We asked her not to touch and to go away, but Giorgio stopped what he was doing with Veruschka and draped some fabric on her, then he cut the cloth and let the girl run away with ‘a custom Giorgio di Sant’Angelo.’”.

#134930. The 7 Lessons I Learned About Skin After Losing 85 Pounds

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1447 w)

The 7 Lessons I Learned About Skin After Losing 85 Pounds

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1447 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Harpersbazaar

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I lost 85 pounds without bariatric surgery.
  • Industry observers note that because I’m losing weight more slowly, I haven’t yet encountered loose skin, though I still have at least 50 more pounds to go.
  • It’s a pretty unsexy topic—which is why it’s rarely, if ever, discussed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I lost 85 pounds without bariatric surgery. Weight loss has been on my mind basically my entire life, especially since I started this journey in earnest in July 2019. And, as proud of myself as I most certainly am for losing this weight and finally getting healthier, it is met toe-to-toe with pervasive anxiety and a nagging question: What about excess skin?

Industry observers note that because I’m losing weight more slowly, I haven’t yet encountered loose skin, though I still have at least 50 more pounds to go. I worry, perhaps too much, about whether I’ll make it to my goal weight without needing skin tightening at the end of this journey.

It’s a pretty unsexy topic—which is why it’s rarely, if ever, discussed. But for those like me who are on major weight-loss journeys, or whose bodies have changed significantly through pregnancy, it’s a question that plagues us: Am I going to encounter excess skin the more weight I lose? And if I do, what can I do about it?

Recent findings suggest that apparently, I’m not the only one with questions, according to New York City plastic surgeon Lara Devgan. “Skin tightening remains one of the elusive black boxes in the world of plastic surgery,” she notes. That mentioned, we’re all still learning about best practices—from me to medical professionals.

So I decided to dig deeper. I rounded up five renowned dermatologists and plastic surgeons from across the country and asked them my questions. And here’s what they have to say.

In a recent development, “Losing weight gradually rather than rapidly may prevent excess skin after major weight loss,” indicates Los Angeles–based dermatologist Harold Lancer. “However, rapid large-scale weight loss will invariably result in excess skin.” Devgan seconds that. “The best way to prevent skin laxity after weight loss is to do your best to lose weight at a slow and steady pace,” she says. “Although it may sound appealing to get to the finish line rapidly, that is actually the worst thing you can do in terms of skin laxity.” Losing weight slowly, she says, allows the skin to contract and shrink as the body shape changes.

Though I personally haven’t opted for weight loss surgery, many do—and there is zero shame in that. But because weight is lost more rapidly after surgery, the likelihood of excess skin increases, so experts recommend pairing weight loss surgery with a skin removal procedure. Why worry about excess skin, especially after faster weight loss? It’s “because collagen and elastin fibers are destroyed when skin is stretched significantly and remains stretched for an extended amount of time,” says Newly introduced York City plastic surgeon David Shafer. “Patients should plan on staged procedures if having a weight loss surgery followed by a skin removal surgery.”.

It has been revealed that “Typically, younger patients with thicker and more sebaceous skin will have more skin contraction during weight loss due to better elasticity,” Devgan says. “Starting in the 20s, tissue elasticity begins to decline. Even in the absence of weight fluctuation, loss of tissue turgor and decreased firmness can be seen in midface descent in the late 20s, breast laxity in the 30s, abdominal laxity in the 40s, and extremity laxity in the 50s.”.

According to recent reports, however, Devgan says everyone’s body is different. “There is a tremendous amount of variability in the human experience, so some patients may lose 50 pounds with minimal change in their body, while others can lose as few as 10 and see tissue laxity.” If you are genetically blessed with unusually superb tissue elasticity, Devgan says, it can be less dramatic. (And lucky you.).

According to recent reports, lifestyle choices can also factor in, Boston-based dermatologist Ranella Hirsch says. How long were you at the weight you started losing from? Are you a smoker? Do you spend a lot of time in the sun without protection? All these factors play into skin elasticity.

Sources indicate that “Using an emollient moisturizer rich in vitamin E will help improve the barrier protection of the skin and lock in moisture,” Devgan says. She also says the topical medical-grade ingredients you use on your face for firmness and tightness—like hyaluronic acid, peptides, niacin, squalene, vitamins C and B, retinol, and bakuchiol—can work elsewhere, too. “Most people focus on using these for the face and neck in their daily routines, but from a molecular perspective, their efficacy is present anywhere on the body.” But save your money on creams that promise you the world. “Losing large amounts of weight rapidly tends to leave skin behind,” Hirsch says. “Though creams with incredible claims abound, they actually do little.”.

Nécessaire The Body Lotion with Niacinamide.

Biossance Squalane + Caffeine Toning Body Cream.

Sol de Janeiro Bom Dia Bright Body Cream with Vitamin C.

Augustinus Bader The Body Cream.

U Beauty The SCULPT Arm Compound Body Serum.

Building muscle through weight training might help reduce the appearance of lax skin, Latest York City dermatologist Dendy Engelman says. “This helps reduce the appearance by replacing the lost fat with muscle mass.”.

Recent findings suggest that nonsurgical options can help with loose skin after weight loss, but they won’t help with skin folds or hanging skin. “Noninvasive treatments such as laser and radiofrequency can help tighten the skin, but there is a limit to how much they can do,” Shafer adds. “Hanging skin generally needs to be surgically excised with procedures such as abdominoplasty, body lift, and arm lift.” Shafer claims there’s a difference between loose skin and hanging skin. “It’s possible patients can manage and treat excess skin cases without undergoing skin removal surgery, such as if the skin is loose but not hanging.” He adds, “In that case, noninvasive treatments may be useful, but hanging skin most often requires surgical excision.”.

Industry observers note that “After major weight loss, people may have skin that hangs off their body,” Engelman states. “These heavy folds can cause health problems such as pain, inflammation, and frequent infections from the skin constantly rubbing together. This can happen during exercise or everyday activities. When a person is having functional problems because of their excess skin, it should be a sign that this problem needs to be addressed.” And, of course, everyone’s journey is different.

Industry observers note that lancer says some individuals will tolerate moderate laxity and be happy with the weight-loss accomplishment; others will seek skin tightening for as little as a five-pound weight loss. But, he says, if plastic surgery does become the option on the table, “I would recommend getting at least three opinions from doctors who exclusively do excess body skin reduction. Once you select a doctor, do one small area on your body, so you can evaluate the procedure, how your body heals, and your results. Afterward, you can determine whether you’d like to proceed with a full-blown larger procedure.”.

According to recent reports, he suggests consulting a dermatologist for nonsurgical options, then asking that doctor to recommend plastic surgeons who specialize in excess body skin reduction if you feel that is the right path for you. This is a major decision and shouldn’t be taken lightly. Bring medical professionals along for the entire weight-loss journey (even if you’ve already started) and ask all the questions: Which specific procedure is best? How much will it cost? Will insurance cover it? (From my research so far, no, if it is cosmetic, but perhaps yes if it would help correct something that limits your daily functionality.) No question is off-limits, and don’t try to make these decisions alone.

It has been revealed that if this piece applies to you at all, whether it’s longstanding weight you carried, weight you lost during pregnancy, or somewhere in between, that means one thing: You’ve taken major steps toward better physical health, and that should be applauded. “Everyone’s weight loss story is different, and some days are harder than others,” Engelman claims. “I say, try to be kind to yourself. You’ve just reached a huge accomplishment and should be proud of that.”.

Industry observers note that devgan agrees. “Accomplishing a personal health goal like major weight loss is an incredible achievement that anyone should be proud of,” she indicates. “While excess skin can feel like a burden or source of self-consciousness, it is also a reminder of the metaphorical and literal shedding of the weight of a prior version of oneself. You cannot have a couture gown without a seam, and you cannot have a surgery without a scar. Life has limitations, but that does not make it less beautiful. It makes it more real.”.
